speechtext: Mr. Speaker, 1 rise on a question of personal privilege. I should like, through you, Mr. Speaker, to ask the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) whether he is prepared today to make a full and unequivocal withdrawal of the charge he made yesterday in the House to the effect that I deliberately misled the House.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: MR. DAVIS-REQUEST THAT MEMBER FOR GANDER-TWILLINGATE MAKE FULL WITHDRAWAL OF CHARGE THAT MINISTER DELIBERATELY MISLED HOUSE
speechtext:
The Minister of Fisheries gave the Chair notice earlier today, as required by the Standing Orders, of his intention to raise this matter again today by way of question of privilege. Since receiving the minister's notice I have looked closely at what was said in debate yesterday when the Chair took exception to a charge made by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate.
After suggestions made by the Chair to the hon. member and to the House in general that a charge that another member deliberately misled the House is unparliamentary, the hon. member, perhaps not to the extent that the Chair would have liked, did say twice or three times that the statement he was making was that the minister had misled the House. It is, of course, well established that in debate a member can say at any time that another member is uttering a misleading statement. That has never been deemed to be unparliamentary.
The question I had to resolve yesterday was whether the withdrawal by the hon. member was satisfactory in view of the precedents and practice of the House. I had urged the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate to make a clear withdrawal. He made a statement which at the time I felt was satisfactory from the point of view of the Chair. I had invited hon. members who felt that perhaps they would like to contribute and give some guidance to the Chair on the matter to do so. I particularly at the time addressed
myself to the Minister of Fisheries, and this did not evoke a response.
Hon. members know the rule to the effect that when a member has a question of privilege to raise it should be done immediately. When the matter in question was first brought up for consideration I had hoped that hon. members who felt they had a question of privilege or wanted to take part in that question of privilege, or who felt they were aggrieved in some way, would have assisted the Chair yesterday, and I doubt very much whether 24 hours later it is possible to revive a question of privilege which has been, in the opinion of the Chair at least, resolved.
The notice I received from the minister includes the suggestion that the matter was left unresolved by the Chair. That was not my impression.

My thought was that, although the amendment or modification which had been made by the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate was not entirely satisfactory, I was willing to accept it. Certainly I believe, in reading the record, I did indicate that so far as I was concerned this was closing the matter, and I did not expect that on a question of privilege the matter would be revived today. I would hope that under the circumstances we could allow the House to go on with its business.
I would like to reiterate what I said yesterday, that the House can operate efficiently only if members are prepared to respect the rules, traditions and practices of the House and to use parliamentary language. It seems to me we can have useful debates, for the benefit of the institution, by limiting ourselves to what are parliamentary expressions. When unparliamentary expressions are used I will consider it my duty to intervene and seek the co-operation of hon. members in using expressions that are accepted as parliamentary. I caution hon. members against excesses in language, and I am sure I will be able to count on their co-operation in the days, weeks or months ahead.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to correct to a certain extent the injustice and the discrimination towards Indian women, resulting from the implementation of section 12 (1) (b) of the Indian Act.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker. I would like to thank the hon. member for Cumberland-Colchester North (Mr. Coates) for accepting the suggestion of the Chair and giving me an opportunity to introduce third reading.
It is now almost nine months, perhaps a little over nine months since this bill received first reading. It was some time back in March and April when the House debated second reading and approved the foreign investment review bill in principle. After that the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs held numerous meetings and received evidence from many persons- spokesmen for business, the labour movement, provincial governments and other interested groups. I and my officials appeared before the committee on several occasions. Subsequently, a number of amendments were proposed by members in committee. Some are now incorporated in the bill. Most are technical in nature. Others are intended to improve the administration of the legislation, and still others deal with such matters as the requirement to take into account provincial representations. This process has given us a better bill. I want to commend the committee for its work and to thank its members for their efforts.
Finally, during the past two weeks the House debated proposed amendments during the report stage, and adopted two of them as recently as yesterday. In short, Mr. Speaker, this bill has been subjected to lengthy and detailed scrutiny by members of the House. The time has now come to give the legislation our approval.
All of you are familiar with the background to the foreign investment review bill-the very high levels of foreign control of Canadian business, and the growing concern of the Canadian people. The work of my colleague, the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray), who has given his name to the most exhaustive study of this area, contributed in a very important way to the understanding by the public of this problem.
The figures on foreign control of Canadian business have been cited many times. This makes them no less important today. They bear repeating. No less than 60 per cent of the capital employed in our manufacturing industries is controlled by foreign businesses. The figures are even higher for particular manufacturing sectors. For
November 20, 1973

example, for rubber it is almost 100 per cent; automobiles and parts, 98 per cent; chemicals, 81 per cent, and electrical apparatus 75 per cent. In petroleum and gas, the comparable figure is 74 per cent, and for other mining 73 per cent. These industries are among the principal goods producing sectors of our economy. They are the engines of our economic growth. They are also the vital base that supports a large part of our service sector. They help to shape the character and quality of employment opportunities available to Canadians.
The Canadian future, Mr. Speaker, is not something that just happens. We, the elected representatives of the Canadian people, have the power, and more than that the obligation to help shape that future, for no country offers a greater opportunity to its citizens to share in building a future. At no time in our history have we had a better opportunity than we have now to build a distinctive Canada. It is our choice if we wish to make it. It is a question of political will, no more, no less. Bill C-132 is an important part in the exercising of that choice, in expressing that political will.
The kind of Canada we want to build must be more than a mere appendage of foreign corporate giants south of the border and the resource hungry multinational firms of other industrialized countries. We must look to the day when these astonishing figures on foreign control are more moderate, when Canadians themselves have an adequate degree of control over the Canadian economy, and when those Canadian firms that are foreign controlled are nevertheless more oriented to the needs and potentials of Canada.
This bill is an important instrument in support of our objectives for Canadian industrial development. As I have said on other occasions, those objectives can be summarized in six propositions: one, the achievement of the maximum attainable levels of employment to match the current and future growth of the labour force; two, the development of an efficient processing and manufacturing industry capable of meeting competition at home and abroad; three, the increased up-grading of our natural resources prior to export to maximize Canada's economic return; four, to provide for greater domestic control of the Canadian economy so as to create conditions conducive to greater Canadian entrepreneurship at home and abroad; five, to increase national income and to provide for regional economic expansion which will reduce regional disparities; six, To contribute to improvement in the quality of life in all parts of Canada by creating satisfying jobs for Canadians and by reducing the harmful effects of industrial activity on the natural and social environment. These six objectives are clearly central to our task.
Just as clearly this bill underlines how inter-connected are our industrial objectives and a coherent set of industrial policies. Our objectives for greater Canadian control of our domestic economy are interwoven with the other objectives. Just as clearly, our policies on foreign investment are interwoven with the other major policy areas. In short to achieve our objectives, to give effect to a coherent set of policies, and to implement our strategies for individual industries we need the passage of Bill C-132. This bill focuses on control, not ownership, because it is the actual power to make decisions rather than the mere
Foreign Investment Review Act fact of share ownership that affects the performance of subsidiaries in Canada.
Federal policy does not aim at cutting Canada off from foreign direct investment. Such investment has played an important role in our past economic development and, in my opinion, certain kinds of foreign investments will continue to have an important contribution to make in our future growth. Let us not forget that we still have the fastest growing labour force in the world. But Canada has also paid a substantial price because of this phenomenon. There are at least two dimensions to these economic costs.
The first is the impact on the general economic environment in Canada, the result of having such a vast proportion of our productive economy controlled by foreign corporations. We have become too accustomed to expecting others to do our research, product innovation and market development, and too accustomed to others telling us what we might do. We have not become nearly accustomed enough to deciding for ourselves what we should do. The degree of foreign control has dulled or inhibited entrepreneurship in Canada by Canadians in Canadian firms. Many Canadians have become too accustomed to playing second fiddle. If we continue to rely so heavily on others, we shall never ourselves become more innovative. If we lose the power to innovate in a changing world we turn over the future development of Canada to those who retain that power.
Earlier this year in Vancouver the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced the government's policy of insisting upon the further processing or upgrading of our natural resources prior to export. In a number of public speeches since that time, I have repeated the importance of this policy announcement and the importance of the bill now before us in giving effect to that policy objective. Under Bill C-132 the foreign investment review agency will have the power to obtain a commitment from a foreign corporation making a direct investment in a Canadian raw material enterprise when that investment involves control.
Similarly, the sourcing of components in Canadian operations-sometimes not too different in principle from raw material development where a foreign investor ships machinery in in order to ship unprocessed raw materials out-will be covered by screening where there are changes of control or foreign control involving the establishment of a new business. One has only to talk to senior officers of many of our leading firms-subsidiaries of foreign parents-to know that they do not have free access to the markets of the world for their products, nor do they have freedom to decide on the products that they will produce in their Canadian factories for distribution in Canada.
The point is simply this: There have been real costs to Canada. Yes, there have been important benefits, too. But our responsibility now is to ensure that we maximize those benefits and minimize those costs for the future industrial development of Canada. Only by conscious and purposeful effort to break this self-perpetuating chain of independence, an effort demanding active and vigorous support by businessmen and government, shall we succeed.

November 20, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
Will the boardrooms of New York, Detroit, London, Dusseldorf and Tokyo recognize Canada's needs and abilities? Will they do so if we do not insist? The answer is clearly, no. Do the decisions of other governments sometimes unreasonably deprive Canadians of legitimate economic opportunities? I think here the record says clearly, yes. These questions could, of course, be asked in relation to international trade as well as international investment. In the case of trade, governments have reached a high degree of agreement on the rules of the game. There are accepted procedures for international negotiation. These procedures assure Canadians that if their government negotiates skilfully, their economic interests will be protected and advanced. The rules of the GATT, while not perfect, provide considerable assurance against a return to the mistakes of the 1930s.
But, in the matter of direct investment, there is no comparable set of rules binding governments or multinational businesses. It is, therefore, not unreasonable for national governments to concern themselves with the impact of direct investment on their national economies. For the Canadian government, in particular, the need to be concerned is especially compelling, in view of the uniquely high degree of foreign control in our manufacturing and resource sectors. The fact is that both the structure and the growth of our economy are heavily influenced by corporate decisions taken outside our border. And these business decisions can be affected by the actions of governments which are not answerable to the Canadian electorate. Canadians want the advantages of international investment, as well as of international trade, and they want access to the new technologies developed elsewhere. But at the same time they want some reassurance that they are not unduly and sometimes detrimentally controlled by forces which they cannot influence. Canadians want to know that they retain considerable independence to determine their future.
Hon. members may be aware that I have spoken on several occasions about the fact that the government's approach on foreign investment rests on two pillars. One pillar is built on that package of policies-tax measures, investment aids, research and development incentives, export assistance, support for small business, are examples-which are aimed at encouraging Canadian businessmen to do more. I shall comment more fully on this aspect of our policy in a few moments.
The second pillar is based on that group of measures which might be called safeguards, those aimed at assuring for Canadians that certain vital national interests will be protected. The Tories would try to put down these safeguard measures down as negative measures. But I say to them that they are positive measures aimed at protecting and developing Canada. To listen to some of the Tories, Mr. Speaker, one would think there should be no restraints, no restrictions; that we do not need restrictions, that there is no reason to screen foreign investment. They say, Mr. Speaker, that they would rely on guidelines and incentives alone. Mr. Speaker, not all hon. members in the Progressive Conservative Party believe that myth but some do, and we have heard it in this House. Some right now are trying to tell me that they believe it. That is the only interpretation I can put on the heckling from across

the floor. Mr. Speaker, I say that these measures are positive measures.
Part of the second pillar has consisted of identifying key sectors of the economy in which it has been necessary to require by law that all, or at least a large proportion of the firms in those sectors, can be Canadian-owned and con-trolled-chartered banks, life insurance companies, other financial institutions-

Yes, such as trust and loan companies, broadcasting and newspapers. Liberal governments have legislated to ensure that in these sensitive areas, Canadian control is dominant. And, as you know, on the matter of foreign ownership of land, it was decided at the last meeting of federal and provincial first ministers to review jointly the legal, constitutional and land use aspects of this question and to consider ways in which the levels of government could co-operate on this problem.
Bill C-132, the Foreign Investment Review Act, signifies an important development of this second pillar of safeguards. One feature that distinguishes this bill from previous legislation is that it will apply across the entire economy and not just to a particular sector. Having described the bill during the debate on second reading and in considerable detail before the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, I shall confine myself today to a brief review of its highlights.
The Foreign Investment Review Act would initially give the government the legal authority to review proposed foreign takeovers of Canadian businesses, above a threshold size. The threshold is not as high as the Tories would like. They wanted to raise that threshold, but they were outvoted when the amendment came before the House a little while ago.

Mr. Speaker, if the hon. member had read the bill he would know the answer to that question. Decisions regarding the impact on employment, efficiency, competition and those other factors to which I referred a few moments ago will be governed by the economic facts. Furthermore, since economic strengths and weaknesses differ from region to region this policy, while national in scope, will be sensitive to differences in the needs of the regions.
I should like to say another word or two about the test of significant benefit. In my view this is central to our policy for Canada and is central to the bill itself. It is essential for two reasons. First, given the present degree of foreign control of the Canadian economy, it seems only reasonable not to allow that degree of foreign control to increase unless foreign investors are in a position to add something of significance to the Canadian economy. To have further increases in foreign control where there are not significant benefits is unacceptable.
Second, the significant benefit test puts the government in the position of being able to bargain to achieve improved benefits from foreign investment, to insist on certain practices or policies by the investor which become his commitment to the government, practices or policies which in the absence of the commitment could be altered at will by the arbitrary decisions of foreign-based businesses or pressures placed on them by foreign governments. We must have some capacity to bargain with investors about their plans for Canada. I expect that we shall be more successful in some cases than in others. The need for the government to intervene, and the capacity to do so effectively, will obviously vary according to the time, the sector and the economic circumstances. However, I have no doubt that the review agency will with perseverance and growing experience, bring to Canada benefits which it would not otherwise have obtained.
There are some people who think that this approach is wrong, that we should replace the significant benefit test with a no detriment test.

I have referred in the past to our foreign investment policy being built upon two pillars, a pillar of safeguard measures of which C-132 is the major part, and a pillar of incentive measures designed to encourage Canadians to save, invest, manage, innovate and develop competitive modern enterprises. Let me refer to some of these other positive measures.
First, Canadian controlled private corporations pay a reduced rate of corporation tax on the first $50,000 a year of income. This reduced rate is 20 per cent on income from manufacturing and processing activities and 25 per cent on income from other activities. This reduced rate is not available to foreign controlled firms. Moreover, the savings from these advantageous rates must be repaid if the firm is transferred to non-Canadian control.
Second, the Canada Development Corporation was established to help develop strong Canadian-controlled businesses and to attract Canadian savings into such development. As is already evident, the CDC is actively at work assisting to promote Canadian ownership and control and a vigorous economy. Although it operates at arms length from the government, the CDC is an outgrowth of a Liberal initiative.
Third, the proposed new Canada business corporations act, Bill C-213, introduced by the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Gray), the man who gave his name to the exhaustive examination of foreign investment in Canada, will require that all federally incorporated foreign-controlled corporations have a majority of directors who are resident Canadians and who are not employees of the corporation or its affiliates.
Let me mention a few other measures that are pertinent. There are some which do not discriminate between Canadian-controlled and foreign-controlled firms, but in fact principally assist Canadian-controlled firms. First, I
November 20, 1973

announced a few months ago plans to revamp and expand the activities of the Industrial Development Bank. The necessary details are now being worked out. The new industrial bank and development agency will build on the accomplishments of the IDB. I think it is perhaps worth reminding hon. members that less than 1 per cent of the loans of the IDB have been made to foreign-controlled firms. This new agency will be more entrepreneurial in its lending and investment activity and will also be a major source of management advice and assistance to small businesses. I expect that the almost exclusive assistance to Canadian-controlled firms will continue.
Second, tax incentives have been implemented to stop the undue leakage of savings from Canada. Pension funds need to retain 90 per cent of their assets in Canada to avoid paying a penalty tax of one per cent per month on those of their assets abroad that exceed 10 per cent of their total assets. The gross-up provisions on Canadian dividends encourage investment in Canadian stocks.
Third, Canadian businesses are able to deduct as an expense the interest paid on funds borrowed to finance the purchase of shares of other firms.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, the catalogue of accomplishments of the Liberal government that I referred to relate mainly to what we have done in the economic sphere. I could have also elaborated at some length on the various measures which have been taken to fortify and encourage Canadian cultural development, the Canadian content provisions in the CRTC regulations, the numerous positive incentives to the film industry and the book publishing industry, programs to foster bilingualism and mul-ticulturalism and the various cultural activities which are supported so effectively through the Canada Council. speechtext:
It is a particular pleasure to enter this debate just after the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) has outlined his views of what this piece of legislation will do for Canada. I consider the outline be has provided to be a devastating indictment of the Liberal party which has held office for 32 of the last 38 years. If this country has gotten into the terrible mess he tells us it is in at the present time, I can only say that the buck stops at the door of the Liberal party, for they are the people who allowed the things he says have happened, to happen.
One of the real problems a member from the maritime provinces faces when he comes to Ottawa lies in differentiating between what is said by cabinet ministers of the Liberal government and the facts as they affect his part of Canada. One of the reasons members from the Atlantic provinces have expressed such deep concern over the legislation presently before the House is that, day in and day out, their constituents encounter the many difficulties which arise in trying to remain part of this nation and trying not to feel they are second class citizens as a result of one action after another which federal governments have taken.
It might not be so great a travesty if the facts were different. But we came into confederation in 1867 as a prosperous area of a new nation. And we have gone downhill steadily ever since. It has been a very difficult role that the people of Atlantic Canada have played as citizens in the development of this nation. But we have stood with this nation. We have never talked about separatism. We have not adopted the sensible words of Joseph Howe when he spoke them in 1867 and warned us about our future. We have watched a tariff system established which has been of tremendous benefit to the central region of the nation but which has done vast damage to the remainder. We have asked over and over again for programs which will improve our position. As a region, we have been studied to death.
Some time ago I asked a question on this matter and I was told there had been some 250 federally-sponsored investigations into the problems which face our area. Yet today, when we look at the various indicators to determine our health as compared with the rest of Canada, we find we are a very sickly part of the nation. We have less of 
everything and we end up paying more for everything we require. It is just great for a minister from Toronto to get up and tell us how he is going to defend us and look after our resources and see that we keep them for our children and their children. But what comes to the minds of most of those who live in Atlantic Canada is this question: How are we going to live and how are our children going to live to enjoy some of the benefits available to the fat cats who live in central Canada, and who are now so concerned about the resources of this country.
We have resources in Atlantic Canada. They are providing jobs today for the people who live in that part of the country. By and large, these resources have been developed as a result of foreign investment. We would be much happier, as I am sure all Canadians would, if Canadian capital were developing our resources. But what we discover is that if foreign investment does not develop our resources, then no investment does. As a result, we are left without jobs for our people, which means they cannot maintain themselves and their families. That is the sad fact of the matter.
It is all very well to run down the multinational corporations and to accuse them of great rip-offs. But off the coast of the Atlantic provinces today a great deal of oil and gas exploration is going on which is proving to be very expensive. If it were not for foreign companies willing to gamble their profits, we would not know whether or not we have a tremendous resource here which, if exploited, will produce jobs and dividends for the people living in Atlantic Canada. So, we welcome such investment. The provincial governments in that part of Canada have indicated their concern about this particular piece of legislation. They are afraid it may deter the kind of investment that we still require in order to provide our people with the things they need and which, as Canadian citizens, they have the right to expect.
The amazing thing I have discovered during the 16 years I have been a member of this House is that, almost without exception, members of parliament from the Atlantic or maritime provinces find that their problems are looked at and appreciated by members from western Canada, and that almost always members from western Canada are talking about the same kind of situation which exists in their regions of Canada. In other words, almost always it is central Canada that finds favour as against the east and the west.

speechtext: The rich get richer.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Let me give the House an example of how the rich do get richer and the poor get poorer. I have before me two newspapers published on the same day, November 15, 1973. One is a Toronto paper, the Globe and Mail, and the other a Nova Scotia newspaper, the Halifax Chronicle-Herald. Both papers are carrying two identical advertisements relating to a Zenith solid state Chromaco-lour II television set. Both advertisements carry the same wording. I might say in passing that I certainly have no complaint about Zenith television sets; I think they are excellent. But in Toronto, one of the television sets pictured costs $719.95; that is the price listed in the Toronto
November 20, 1973

Globe and Mail. This same set costs in Halifax $829.95, or $110 more. The price of the other television set shown in the Toronto paper costs $789.95, and there is a little asterisk which denotes this is the suggested retail price. The price in the other paper of this same set is $869.95, in other words $80 more.
It might be said that transportation cost is the reason for the difference. Yet this smaller set that costs $719.95 in Toronto and $829.95 In Halifax is lighter in weight than the other one which costs $80 more. Whatever the reason is, all I can say is that it is just one more symptom of the sickness in this nation which means if you live in the Maritimes, where your pay cheque is less, you pay more for the goods you feel you require. The story is probably exactly the same in Winnipeg, Edmonton, Vancouver and Calgary. This is just one example that a constituent of mine has brought to my attention. We are living in a time of spiralling inflation, with costs increasing all across the nation, yet we in the maritime provinces pay even more than someone living in central Canada. In my opinion there are other basic matters requiring a great deal more priority than investment coming into this nation to create jobs for people who require them. Certainly, transportation is one of the matters that requires action, but action is not forthcoming.
This government has held office for 32 of the last 38 years. It seems that all of the things that it did not do during those 32 years it is now going to correct with this particular piece of legislation, though I do not know how and neither, I am sure, does the government. When the government does try to bring equality to the people of this nation I suggest this area should be number one on the list.
During the 1968 election campaign the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) talked a great deal about the just society. The just society just did not happen in his first four years in office, and it was not even mentioned during the last election campaign. The Prime Minister also talked about regional economic disparity, and some action has been taken in that regard, though not nearly as much action as should have been taken when one considers the kind of investment the government has made in the programs of that particular department. However, there has been some forward movement. Whether the federal government considers itself the main proponent of the improvements that have been made, and thereby the recipient of the kudos arising therefrom, is not really important. Although conditions are improving slightly, a great deal more improvement still needs to be made before we have anything like equality of opportunity.
The minister mentioned some of the areas in which he considered the government had taken action to protect Canadians and to maintain the Canadian heritage for future generations. I suggest that if he is anxious to see the Canadian heritage retained for Canadians there are certain areas in which he and his government should move, and should have moved long before now. We are faced today with a tremendous energy crisis. The minister could have assisted Canadians to enjoy a part of their own heritage had he agreed last January to the extension of the oil pipeline to Montreal. He did not do that, and this
Foreign Investment Review Act winter we must depend on other countries and their decisions for the necessary oil and gas to heat our homes.
I suggest that the minister and his government should also take another look at the tremendous coal reserves in this country. It is suggested they are in the neighbourhood of 120 billion tons. The government should do something about making this coal marketable in order that Canadians could produce the energy required to manufacture goods and produce the employment we need. Since confederation, more than 100 years ago, we have used less than one billion tons of coal in this nation. In other words, we have used just one per cent of our recoverable coal resources. As a result of the energy crisis, the President of the United States has undertaken a $3 billion research program in respect of their coal reserves in an attempt to find ways and means of gasifying the coal to produce the energy they require to become self-sufficient in the energy field by 1980. That is an example of what that country is doing in order to meet its energy crisis.
Much of our coal is located in the Atlantic area. Coal can be produced by the conventional methods, but we should also consider these resources from the point of view of gasification, cutting down the cost of production and other things of that nature. This can be done with the proper type of research. The minister has not said one word in this regard, except that the coal fields in my constituency, which other Liberal governments have closed down, should be reopened. Certainly, they should be reopened on the basis of conventional coal mining, and we should also look for other ways of deriving benefits from this resource.

The government is waiting for foreign investors, just as we in the Atlantic provinces are waiting for foreign investors to develop the tremendous energy potential from the Fundy tides. This is a gigantic project of the magnitude of the Churchill and lower Churchill Falls combined. It is comparable to the development undertaken in Quebec at James Bay. I was informed last week by the government, through the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald), that after two years of re-examining a study produced in 1969, which indicated that the Fundy tidal power project was feasible from an energy point of view but not from an economic point of view, perhaps there will be another investigation carried out to determine further aspects of this project. The Premier of Nova Scotia recently suggested that this new study, which could cost another $1 million, might be a good thing. Foreign Investment Review Act give Canadians incentives to invest in this country rather than making conditions attractive to foreign investment.
In 32 of the 38 years we have had a Liberal government, Canadians have been coddled to the extent they see nothing but mortgages and bonds in which to invest their money. They are afraid to take a chance, and I do not blame them if they have money invested in projects of this government. We should provide great incentives to Canadians to invest in Canada. We should make sure that they can obtain reasonable returns on their capital, while at the same time helping their fellow citizens toward a better way of life. This is what our party stands for; an incentive society in which people take advantage of incentives provided by the government. This government should provide incentives rather than detriments.

I suggest we should rip-off this government in order to derive some benefit from the tremendous number of tax dollars that have been invested over the years. What better opportunity could we provide our citizens than tax incentives to encourage investment in this country. We should encourage Canadian investment to an extent comparable to foreign investment with comparable benefits.
I should like to make one or two remarks about land ownership. For some time I have been concerned, as a maritimer, about land ownership. I am not speaking as a member from the Atlantic provinces, but as a maritimer representing the view of the people of an area which has been a part of Canada for a long time. We lived, grew up and tried to get our children to grow up in that part of Canada even though we knew they could probably do better if they went somewhere else. But we did it for a great many reasons, and one of them certainly is the grandeur of the land itself.
We have discovered that people who went to the asphalt jungles of North America are now coming back to our part of Canada and are endeavouring to take us to the cleaners because they have made a lot of money. They can afford to offer us a sum of money for our land that we cannot refuse because we are not in the same league as they are. As a result, much of the recreational land that is associated with our way of life in the maritime provinces is being gobbled up by speculators from other parts of Canada and North America. I am pleased that the provincial governments are finally moving in this area, because we have only a limited amount of land and in my opinion our people have the right to first enjoyment of it. From that point of view, I do not mean that we should stop Canadians having cottage land or we should stop Americans and people from other countries buying a piece of land here and enjoying the scenery that we know so well. But I do believe we should put a stop to the kind of speculation that has been going on and that will increase if we do not do something about it.
I think there should probably be a national policy in this regard; but more important than that, there must be provincial government policies to see that our people who stay in the Maritimes and accept a life that is not as fruitful, from a financial point of view, as that available to those who live in other areas, have a right to the enjoy-

ment of that land 12 months of the year, and not to have fences put up and access eliminated to the very best recreational areas and to the surrounding ocean.
I want to conclude by saying that, so far as I am concerned, there are many pieces of legislation that this parliament could be considering that are a lot more important to people in the Atlantic provinces than the measure we are considering. At the same time, I would like to say that I am deeply concerned about any type of roadblock that is put in the way of investment in our area until we at least have an unemployment rate that is on a par with the rest of the nation.
I also think there must be a tremendous amount of guaranteed co-operation between the provincial and the federal governments. I regret very much that some of the proposals made by my colleagues, especially by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay), have not been acceptable to the government. I would be much happier with an incentive type of bill that would convince Canadians that there are many reasons why they should be investing in this country rather than in another country, and that many good dividends are available to them if they do.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take part in this debate for a very short intervention which will last not later than six o'clock, because of the view which my colleagues and I take of the importance of the issue of foreign control of Canada's economy. As I have travelled across this country in the last number of months, I have been very impressed by the fact-and it is a fact-that ever-growing numbers of Canadians in every part of Canada are deeply concerned about the foreign control of Canada's economy and about the impossibility of envisaging a future for Canada which is shaped by Canadians themselves if this foreign control continues at its present level, let alone if it is permitted to increase.
I do not think we can exaggerate the losses to Canada flowing from the fact that our economy in its most important aspect is in the hands of multinational corporations. Whether you look at the fact that our natural resources are yanked out of the earth and shipped across with very little processing, and the consequent loss of development and jobs in Canada; whether you look at the fact that little research and development is done in this country, that almost all of it is done at the headquarters of the parent corporations which control Canada's economy; whether you look at the danger that always faces a Canadian worker in a multinational corporation in Canada; whether you look at the fact that a multinational corporation may find it more economic to transfer its activities not only to the United States but to anywhere in the world, to Singapore, to Africa or elsewhere where they now have plants, and the danger to the jobs of Canadians in those situations-in our present society you will find that the moguls of industry have an immense influence on the ethos of society and on the standard of values by which society is governed.
This is a fact which I regret very much. They have an immense influence on the cultural and spiritual essence of a society as well as in the material and economic sense. When you look at all these aspects that are affected, indeed influenced and governed by the economic power
November 20, 1973

which is now in the hands of multinational corporations, you find that no Canadian who looks ahead, who is not blinded by his subservience to the so-called free enterprise system, can fail to be concerned about our country's present situation.
It took many years for the Liberal government of this country, and the Conservative government before it, to realize the dangers we were facing. If I may say so without, I hope, being improper, some of us saw this many decades ago. It has been drawn to my attention that in a speech I made back in 1956 which was published in pamphlet form-I had forgotten about it until it was drawn to my attention-I gave a warning to Canadians about the foreign control of our economy. My colleagues and I have been warning Canadians for many years about it, not because I like an exploiting Canadian corporation any better than an exploiting multinational one but because multinational control carries with it consequences beyond mere economic questions in a country.
Finally, after years of study, the government brought down a bill in the last parliament which we were determined to stymie, a bill which did nothing at all, which dealt with perhaps 2 per cent or 3 per cent of the problem that is before us. But this year, undoubtedly because of the minority situation of the government, it has produced a bill that is considerably stronger. Instead of dealing only with foreign takeovers, it deals also with new businesses of foreigners and with the expansion of existing corporations in unrelated areas.
The minister has accepted some changes which my colleagues on the committee suggested, which have also served to strengthen the criteria which are to govern the agency and the government in making decisions under the bill. Because it has been considerably strengthened, we have said from the start that we would not block the passage of this bill and would vote for it. However, I want to make clear, Mr. Speaker, that we are under no illusions that Bill C-132 is more than a short step in the right direction. This is the main reason for my taking part in the debate at this stage.
The bill still does not deal with the most important part of the problem in Canada, which is the expansion of existing foreign corporations in this country. Even the present bill will deal only with 10 per cent to 20 per cent of the problem, depending on what happens in a given year, and the remaining problem will not be touched. The minister has again indicated with figures the extent of this problem. There is over 70 per cent foreign ownership in mining, and in certain manufacturing industries almost 100 per cent. It is almost 100 per cent in the automotive industry, and 90 per cent ownership of the natural resources of this country, including the energy resources to which I will return in a moment. There is something like 80 per cent foreign ownership of the refining facilities in this country. The minister quite rightly emphasized that all these important levers of economic control-"important" is almost an understatement-these almost overwhelming levers of economic control are now in the hands of multinational corporations.
