Mr. Speaker, recently the people of Quebec were given a choice, for or against Canada. Overwhelmingly they opted for Canada. It was not easy, I am sure, for those who had supported the Party Creditiste or l'Union Nationale for long years, and some of their parents before them, not to support those parties in the election. It was not easy, I am sure, for many who for social or economic reasons, would have supported the Parti Quebecois to opt for Canada. Many others who supported the Parti Quebecois did so because they liked its economic and social views; they would not have supported the party if asked to vote on a referendum. The people of Quebec, Mr. Speaker, have opted for Canada. I am firmly convinced that if the rest of the people of Canada were given the same opportunity, they too would most certainly respond in like manner.
If there is one single issue which would catch the fancy of all Canadians, whether from Quebec or British Columbia, from Newfoundland or Ontario, from Alberta or any other part of the land, that issue would be the opportunity to opt for Canada and for the independence and the integrity of the nation.
I am not suggesting, Mr. Speaker, that the foreign investment review bill is by any means the vehicle which

November 20, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act would catch the fancy of all Canadians. It is not that kind of bill. It is not that far reaching; it is not that exciting; it is not that stirring. None the less, it is, I believe, an extremely significant piece of legislation. It is significant, I submit, in two respects. First, it enables us to stand up and be counted. Second, it sets up a good mechanism which, if extended, could have a really important effect on all foreign investment in Canada.
As we approach the vote on third reading I should like briefly to review the status of foreign ownership in Canada at this time. With respect to foreign ownership, this country is perhaps like no other in the western community in the degree of equity ownership which we allow to outsiders. Most countries either limit ownership or take funds in the form of bonds or other non-equity or portfolio capital. Britain, for instance, financed a great deal of North and South American growth in the pre-first world war era with this type of investment.
The extent of foreign ownership in Canada in many areas of the economy is well known. I will mention only two or three areas. When we look at manufacturing, we are talking of foreign ownership in the area of 65 to 70 per cent. About the same amount of our mining is foreign-owned. When we consider petroleum and the petrochemical industry, we must concede that between 80 and 90 per cent of the industry is foreign-owned. That shows the extent of foreign ownership affecting our various industries. In addition, we must consider the matter of control. Much of the Canadian portion of the manufacturing industry, and particularly of the petroleum industry, is held in the form of preferred stock and not in the form of voting or controlling stock. That is the situation in this part of the 1970s.
A great deal of concern has been expressed in this debate and in committee hearings about the need for foreign investment. Without question, our affluence up to now has depended upon a great deal of money coming in from outside. I question, at this point, whether this is still true. Let me first of all say that I wish to ease the concern of some hon. members from the have-not provinces. I will mention this later. I know that some of those members are concerned that possibly their provinces will suffer if less foreign investment comes into the country.
Let me mention some figures. According to the latest American figures available to me, during the five years 1966 to 1970, $2.2 billion U.S. was directly invested in Canada. The outflow to the United States in the form of dividends, rents, etc., was $5.5 billion. Further, during that period U.S. interests acquired an additional $7.4 billion of assets in this country. In other words, for every dollar that entered Canada from the United States-this does not include money coming from Japan, Germany, or other areas-$2.50 went out in dividends and American interests acquired $4 worth of assets or equities. In other words, outside groups are buying Canada with our money.
I mentioned concerned groups. Perhaps the most significant group we dealt with in committee were some of the provinces which are not as well off as a province such as Ontario. I can understand the concern of these provinces. They fear that in some way or another foreign investment

will decrease because of this bill. That is misplaced concern. At the very beginning of the second reading debate there was a lot of talk about the term "significant benefit". There are those who would like to water the words "significant benefit" down to "benefit". It seems extremely important to have the words "significant benefit" in the bill. What might only be of benefit to a province like Ontario could be very significant to a province like New Brunswick or some other province where the amount of investment is not as great.
The Minister of Regional Economic Expansion (Mr. Jamieson) made a statement which impressed me very much. He talked about the kinds of foreign investments that are made in the poorer provinces. Generally, these are in raw materials and do not create many jobs. The processing is not done in the province. As the minister indicated, as soon as there is some slightly adverse situation, as was the case with the three fish producing plants in the Mari-times, the companies disappear as soon as prices become poor. The disadvantaged parts of Canada should not be concerned. They should welcome this bill. In many cases it is a way of attracting investment to those areas.
The other group which seems to be concerned includes some of the large corporations, some of which are multinational, some major oil companies and some real estate companies and other important groups in our corporate sector. There was one group of 32 companies of which one-half were Canadian-owned. The people who represented them were from companies where the majority ownership was American. In spite of the testimony, this bill will be an advantage to Canadian firms in this group. In a case where there is not significant benefit for an American firm to buy out a Canadian firm, that firm would not be able to do so. A Canadian firm in competition, trying to buy out the same company, would have an advantage. This bill, rather than being detrimental to the have-not provinces or the Canadian portion of the corporate sector, should be of real benefit.
There is one problem with this bill that has been cited by members of the New Democratic Party. It has to do with the fact it does not make provision for companies already functioning in Canada to expand. I can fully understand the concern of the minister in expressing the difficulty one would have in defining expansion. Where does expansion start and where does it stop? As a government, I do not think we are relying on this bill to prevent this kind of expansion or to increase Canadian ownership. There are other ways of doing that, and I wish to suggest one or two. First, the provinces must be concerned about land sales. I understand that in northwestern Ontario, in the area around Thunder Bay in particular, 10 per cent of the surveyed land is owned by nationals of another country; they are mostly American. The province of Ontario has had a select committee seriously considering legislation to correct this type of situation.
There is a whole series of areas where tax incentives can increase Canadian ownership. Many have suggested these. I do not intend to get into them at this time. The Canada Development Corporation is to be congratulated on its efforts in acquiring a principal holding in Texasgulf. There will be many more opportunities in the future to acquire control of other large corporations working in
November 20, 1973

Canada. This should not be taken as a threat; it will come about in a very natural way.
There has been a tendency to look at all incoming capital as being always welcome. When we get into the whole area of energy with up to $100 billion in capital flowing into Canada in the next 15 years, it will have a very serious effect on the Canadian dollar, pushing it up considerably. It will also have a very serious effect in terms of purchase of energy. In other words, if the United States or other countries buy Canadian energy excessively, they will not be in a position to buy other manufactured goods. The Economic Council dealt with this question in its recent publication. This excess inflow would be significant enough that we could in some way or other arrange for a portion of it to be turned back in the form of equity. The same thing that Britain did between the wars and during World War II might occur. The Americans might well sell some of their equity to maintain a stable dollar and a stable trade relationship.
There is another field in which we can expand our Canadian ownership, control and input. This relates to the whole field of energy. There are those who ask why energy should be singled out as being different from manufacturing or any other sector of the economy. The present energy crisis tells us why. If, for example, the manufacture of plastics became a problem, we could survive. However, I am not sure we can survive without an adequate supply of energy. We must take a special look at this area. We must first become self-sufficient.
We must be able to control our energy supplies. That does not mean we should not sell excess energy; that is not the case at all. However, we must become self-sufficient. We must also have a single-price system across this country. To do this we need a national marketing board. This could be set up without too much difficulty. I think negotiations in this area, especially with the province of Alberta, are forthcoming. I talked about this before in terms of a quid pro quo.
Perhaps one of the most important steps that we must take is to set up a national petroleum corporation. That is an area in which it is important we act.
I think, too, we must acquire our own pipelines. We must ensure that our supplies are secure. I would be much more interested in a pipeline from Sault Ste. Marie to Montreal than a pipeline from Montreal through Toronto looping to Sarnia. It seems to me that if a pipeline were routed to Montreal from Sault Ste. Marie, with a short bridge to St. Ignace, a distance of 30 or 40 miles, we would be halfway toward completing a pipeline; and then the second link could be routed from Manitoba to Thunder Bay and around to Sault Ste. Marie. I understand the distance is about the same from Montreal to Sarnia as from Sault Ste. Marie or St. Ignace to Montreal.
Lastly, I think we should be most concerned to acquire and control the whole operation of the tar sands in the Canadian interest. The tar sands area has to be Canada's most valuable piece of real estate. This is not an energy debate and I do not intend to elaborate on this aspect, but I think it is very important for the people of Canada to acquire a considerable interest in this development, either
Foreign Investment Review Act through a national petroleum corporation in some other way, by arrangement with the province of Alberta. These are five or six ways in which we could extend Canadian interest in her own resources.
There is a popular fallacy that those who talk about being Canadian or acquiring an interest in Canada through Canadian ownership are anti-American. This label, which is immediately imposed upon them, is ridiculous. In the field of energy, I do not think anyone is suggesting we are cutting off oil supplies to the Americans. We are shipping over a million barrels a day to them, and to date I am aware of no proposals that this supply should be cut off at least for several years.
A national petroleum corporation should certainly not be a threat to foreign countries. It would create more competition-but competition is what makes the world go round. After all, British Petroleum is a nationally-owned company in competition with United States firms. The multinational corporations in the oil industry and elsewhere are used to tough rules in various countries, and to judge from some conversations I have had, I think they wonder how it is that Canadians are so easy to deal with in this respect. The changes proposed in this bill before us are not such as to create basic animosity. We must remember, as the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Wool-liams) reminded us, that other nations besides the United States are also becoming very large investors in Canada, and that funds of those countries might possibly replace American sources some day. I am thinking particularly of Japan and West Germany.
I have followed the debate in this House on both energy and foreign takeovers. There is one characteristic which I have noticed among spokesmen for the Conservative Party particularly-a constant reference to consulting with the provinces. I accept the need for consultation, but we cannot allow consultation with the provinces to mean the balkanization of Canada. Canada is far more than the sum of its parts and it is extremely important that politicians understand this. We must make decisions here. We will consult in the sense that we will find out how the provinces feel, but the decisions made by the government must be made for the good of all Canadians. Consultation is excellent as a way of finding out; but to the extent that it leads to balkanization-no.
In conclusion, I support this bill, partly because it gives us a good mechanism; but also because it gives us a chance to stand up and be counted. We have dealt with matters such as over-consultation with the provinces, such as reducing the word "significant" or taking it out of the phrase "significant benefit." We resisted these efforts because we felt we must be counted for Canada. This is a beginning, which will be followed by other actions particularly affecting energy policy. However, I think this measure is the beginning of an opportunity for Canadians to opt for the integrity of Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it was a very real privilege to hear the minister speak this afternoon. Always I have believed that what this government does is marked by the style rather than the substance. The speech we heard this afternoon has turned this belief into an unalterable fact based upon experience.

November 20, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
In his opening remarks, the minister said the bill was intended to provide opportunity for building our future and that it was a question of political will, no more and no less, that this be done. He then proceeded to list the problems which many people feel accompany foreign ownership-the dulling of entrepreneurship, control of markets, control of machinery purchases, control of component purchases. He then outlined the steps taken or promised-an increase in the number of Canadian directors until they constituted a majority, Canadian resources being refined in this country, an interest advantage in taxation matters. He referred to the role of the Industrial Development Bank and of the Canada Development Corporation in glowing terms and listed again the priorities set up by his department.
In school, years ago, we were taught to make precis. It would be interesting to determine which part of the minister's rhetoric related to the bill, which to the ideals that are not being met, and which to programs purloined from other sources but claimed now as Liberal achievements. The bill does not deal with the extent of present foreign investment or its expansion within the economy in any way, as long as the expansion is related to an existing undertaking. It does not provide better opportunities for the Canadian entrepreneur in any way-and this is not as dulled as the minister implied; it is simply unable to obtain capital in many instances. The measure before us does nothing to encourage or assist these men who wish to play their role in building Canada.
Claims have been made that the bill embodies innovative provisions including, as I have mentioned, arrangements for Canadians to be in the majority on boards of directors, tax relief in the field of interest, and increased local refining of Canadian resources. Mr. Speaker, these ideas are all taken from actions first carried out in Ontario by a Conservative government. This applies also to the reference which was made to the Prime Minister's speech in Vancouver. None of this is Liberal in origin.
Portions of the minister's speech related to significant benefit and cabinet responsibility. This same gentleman and his fellows presided over the disposition of Supertest Petroleum Corporation, an Ontario-based firm. Granted, the present bill was not then law but the cabinet would, presumably, act on the same basic principles. But though this was a Canadian company, although it was profitable, it was allowed to be sold to a foreign concern, ironically; a company owned and controlled by the government of a foreign country. The minister says it is a question of will, and I agree with him. But the will of this government is lacking, as it has been in the past, and all the will in the world cannot add solid meat to the sawdust that is represented in the minister's speech.
There is no will in this government except to survive, and it hopes the Canadian people will look no further than the rhetoric and not look for the meat. But they will not be so easily fooled as this. They will opt for Canada and for policies that give incentives to Canadians, not for hollow style that is aimed at grabbing headlines and providing grist for candidates trying to prove that their government has done something, that something has been accomplished.

There are a number of important aspects of the control of foreign investment in Canada that must be clearly stated. Investment in the past has been beneficial. It has provided jobs for Canadians, which in its time was a fair bargain in view of the profit and increasing equity gained through such investment. Presently, however, little new money is coming into Canada relative to increased foreign control. In fact, most expansion is financed by Canadian savings, which year by year are becoming more and more adequate and capable of financing our own growth.
Canadian funds are being used to finance the takeover of Canadian companies by those whose primary interest is not necessarily the expansion of jobs in Canada and Canadian markets but, rather, increasing profits to send home. These are companies that look at the world not from a "Canada first" point of view, but from a multinational point of view in which Canada is merely one pawn in a widespread game.
This bill will not necessarily prevent the growth of foreign ownership in new industries. It most certainly will in no way place Canadians at any advantage compared to these many companies presently foreign-owned. Neither will it in any way encourage or assist Canadians either in buying or in retaining their interest in Canadian firms. It will, in effect, give the appearance of action, but will do little except build another department of government that will seem to be active but which in reality will not be. It will simply let the government convince those who are unwary that something has been done when it has not.
However, this bill is better than nothing at all, for the government at least will have to relate its actions to the act and the guidelines under the act, rather than to its own ad hoc actions, as has been the case in the past. But the legislation will do nothing constructive.
Although Canadians, particularly Niagarans, are presently, quite rightly, primarily concerned about rising prices and the energy crisis, there is no doubt that one of their greatest continuing concerns is the question of who will control our destiny. This government has failed in controlling inflation and in developing a rational, planned energy policy. It has also failed during its ten years of existence to address itself in any positive manner to this continuing concern of all Canadians.
The role of the government should be to assist Canadians who are willing to undertake risk, people who are willing to operate companies that can compete for sales at home and abroad and are willing to invest in the enterprise of others. Vast sums have been loaned to countries other than Canada at interest rates lower than Canadian citizens can obtain from the Export Development Corporation, indeed at lower interest rates than the Industrial Development Bank, which the minister boasts about, have offered. This is not just. Many millions have been spent on programs that are of no long-term benefit, often of little short-term benefit and at times of potential or real harm to our society. Could not these funds have been better employed in assisting Canadian enterprise to become more productive and competitive, thus opening up permanent jobs?
A Canadian Development Corporation has been established, but it has not as yet assisted small businessmen to any significant degree to obtain the equity capital which
November 20, 1973

they need. Nor has it reached out in any way to the citizens of Canada, allowing them to assist in building a stronger Canada through personal involvement. The Canadian Development Corporation was claimed by the minister to be an achievement, but as yet it has not touched the citizenry of Canada. This is provided for in the act, so why has it not been done?
Over the years I have sought the opinions of the citizens of Niagara riding and their position was always clear. In the year since they saw fit to place me in this House, the message has become even clearer. Canadians, at least those in Niagara riding, are looking for leadership in regaining control of our economic destiny. They are looking for positive action and are willing to become involved themselves if given the opportunity and support that only the government can provide.
In summation, this bill does not in any way alter the situation of foreign investment in Canada, as it now stands. It is window-dressing that few who are really concerned will be satisfied with. Lastly, it is clear that Canadians who are looking for effective action that will be of assistance to them and will allow them to become involved in this greatest of all problems, that of our independent economic survival, will have to wait still longer than they have already. They will have to wait until the day when the positive programs of the Conservative Party are put forth in the form of government bills. Clearly, the minister does not have the political will to provide the opportunity for Canadians to share in building their future. Just as clearly, a Conservative government, when in power, has that will and will put it into law.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, over the last few months we have been spending many hours discussing Bill C-132. First of all, we dealt with the second reading stage and then had 30 to 40 meetings of the committee; then it came back at report stage, and finally this evening we have reached third reading stage of the bill. During its progress through the House, the committee of the House was able to get three or four amendments put into the bill which, in my opinion, strengthen the bill. Foreign ownership in this country is a very important question. This bill goes part way toward solving at least some of the problems of foreign ownership. It is a small step. It will deal with between 10 and 20 per cent, depending on the year, of foreign activity in Canada and I think it is the first step toward seriously repatriating the Canadian economy.
Canada, perhaps more than any other country, is dependent upon foreign capital. According to Statistics Canada, we now have in excess of $50 billion worth of foreign funds in this country. About 80 per cent of these funds come from the United States of America. On the other hand, as of 1970 Canada had about $6 billion invested in other countries. The reason that the issue of foreign ownership concerns me is really threefold. First of all, we are exporting capital from Canada today. We are a net exporter of capital, not a net importer of capital any longer. As a matter of fact, last year Canada exported some $2.3 billion of capital in the form of dividends, profits and interest rates to United States corporations alone.
Foreign Investment Review Act

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: And union dues.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Perhaps there were union dues as well, though I do not have the statistics for them. But in the form of interest rates, dividends and profits, $2.3 billion went to United States corporations. Yesterday there was a story in the press to the effect that at the rate of outflow of funds, this year probably $2.8 billion of Canadian funds will go to United States investors. As I have said, about 80 per cent of the foreign ownership in Canada is United States investment, and I take it a lot of money in the form of dividends, profits, and so on, also flows out to investors in Japan, Germany, Britain or wherever those investors live.
The second matter that concerns me about the tremendous intensity of foreign ownership of our economy is that I think in the long run it hurts us in terms of jobs. We now have a branch plant economy that depends on the parent plant in many cases to make decisions that effect our economy. Thirdly, I believe that because of the tremendous influx of foreign capital into this country, some of our political and economic decision-making powers have been eroded. Our future is genuinely at stake. I know some people tend to look at some of us as narrow nationalists. I do not think we are. But if you are faced with a choice between nationalism or annihilation as a nation, one would come down on the side of a person who is a nationalist in so far as wanting Canada to develop its own economy in the world community, with the strength to make political and economic decisions.
I become very annoyed at times when I hear members of the Conservative Party suggest we in this party are antiAmerican. I am not anti-American, and I do not blame Americans for what has happened in Canada. I blame two groups for what has happened.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: The Grits.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: I blame the Grits and other governments of this country, including the Tory governments, for the lack of foreign ownership legislation which we should have on our statute books. We have been selling ourselves out; we have been economic prostitutes, so to speak.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Shame.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
We have allowed foreign investors to come into our country, with very few rules or guidelines, to do to us almost anything they want. Secondly, I blame the multinational corporations or the transnational conglomerates which have established themselves around the world. They are vertically integrated and massive in their power. Many of them are much more powerful than the economies of entire countries; some of them more powerful than the economy of Canada. Huge, multinational corporations can affect the economic pattern of the world, the value of various currencies and the balance of payments of many countries. These are the people I blame for the type of situation we face today.
As I have already indicated, the bill before us has a couple of major deficiencies. It does not go far enough because it pertains only to takeovers and new invest-

November 20, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act ments. The bill is, in my opinion, too subjective and leaves too much of the decision-making process to the proposed agency. In some cases that might be good, but you might have an agency which is not too concerned about the question of foreign ownership in Canada and because of its subjectivity there might not be many positive decisions taken. As I said earlier, this bill deals with only 10 per cent or 20 per cent of foreign activity in Canada. It deals with takeovers, new investments and the expansion of existing firms into non-related areas; and this is where you run into trouble. How do you define what is a non-related area? You probably define it by product. Many of our multinational corporations are vertically integrated and are involved in literally hundreds of products.
Let us take the IT&T as an example. It has 58 different subsidiaries operating in this country, involved in literally hundreds of products from toilet paper to telephones. They are involved in the hotel-motel business, the rent-a-car business and many other businesses in Canada. IT&T could literally expand into almost any product in this country and not be screened, because it would be expanding into a related area of one of its subsidiaries.
The same is true of almost any huge, transnational conglomerate now operating in this country. Let us consider Imperial Oil as an example of what I fear. Imperial Oil is operating now in the gas and oil business. However, it is involved in mining, manufacturing, the finance service industry, the wholesale and retail business in this country, in trade, transportation, utilities, construction and pipelines. It is also involved in many other areas and could expand into the binder twine and rope industry in Canada because one of its wholly-owned subsidiaries Polytwine, a company which manufactures rope. Imperial Oil could, through this subsidiary, expand into the twine and rope business. These are the things that concern me about the bill before us. I think it has many loopholes.
Gulf Oil could manufacture as much toothpaste as it wanted, as it is now manufacturing toothpaste in this country through a subsidiary and could further expand in this field. When one travels on an airline he often uses little plastic dishes; they are manufactured and processed by one gas and oil company. One can see that when we start to screen these companies which expand into unrelated areas, because of the vertical integration we will have a difficult time blocking or screening the expansion. Many of them are intertwined and greatly vertically integrated. Bell Canada controls Northern Electric, and Northern Electric controls Microsystems. Microsystems can manufacture a number of devices for Bell Canada; therefore Bell Canada can get into many related businesses through Microsystems.
These are some of the problems I see in the bill before us. I have given a number of reasons why we in this House should strengthen our foreign ownership legislation and should treat this bill as only a first step toward repatriating the economy of Canada so that we, as Canadians, have control of our own destiny. In the next few minutes I want to deal with what I think are two myths constantly referred to in the debate by members of the Conservative Party and many people who are afraid of stronger foreign ownership legislation in this country.

I see that the hon. member for Crowfoot (Mr. Horner) has just entered the chamber.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: He has been here all evening.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: No he hasn't.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Some of the arguments used by that hon. member are along the lines about which I have spoken. One of the myths is that Canada needs more foreign capital if we are to develop. The second myth follows directly from the first, that without foreign capital we would have more unemployment and less development. These are two myths about which the people of Canada should be aware. First of all, as hon. members have pointed out, we are financing our own takeover. Study after study has revealed that of the new foreign expansion in Canada each year, only about 6 per cent has been carried out with funds from abroad and the remaining 94 per cent has been carried out with capital raised in Canadian money markets, through Canadian banks or from profits and retained earnings reinvested in this country. In other words 94 per cent, if not more, of foreign investment is now being accomplished with Canadian funds.
We are using the savings of many ordinary citizens of this country to finance huge, foreign conglomerates which are expanding their industries in Canada, draining off many of their dividends to the foreign parents whether they be United States corporations or companies of other countries. The annual outflow of funds this year, in terms of dividends, interest payments, and so on, is expected to be about $2.8 billion. During the decade of the sixties there was a net export of capital from Canada of about $2 billion. There is more capital flowing out of this country than there is coming in.
We have the money in this country, but we are a net exporter of capital because so much of our industry is foreign-owned. This capital investment is becoming more of a disadvantage than an advantage to us because the percentage of outflow, in terms of capital, is increasing each year. To realize this fact one has only to read the annual statements of various organizations. For example, for the years 1962 to 1971 the payment of interest and dividends to foreign companies increased by some 90 per cent, and from 1967 to 1971 managements fees to parent companies from branch plants increased by 60 per cent. We find that the return on the foreign investment dollar in this country is continually increasing. According to the Shultz report on the Alberta oil and gas industry, for every U S. dollar invested in Alberta since the Leduc find, there has been a return of 71 cents since the first year of the investment.
We find that foreign investment is very profitable for those who are investing in other countries. In the United States, for example, between 1960 and 1967-during that seven-year period-Americans invested around the world some $19.4 billion. The returns on their investments were some $33.3 billion. In Latin-America, during the same seven years, Americans invested $1.7 billion and their returns on those investments were some $8.8 billion. So you can see once again that the people who are helped most by foreign investment are those who are doing the
November 20, 1973

investing, and not the country where the investment is taking place. It is about time Canada grew up and started to repatriate our economy so that we controlled it, and not the foreign corporations.
We find, for example, that our banks and our financial institutions are largely responsible for the sell-out of our country. About $2 billion to $3 billion of Canadian savings was lent to expand foreign activities in this country between 1960 and 1967. Between 1965 and 1969, the Canadian bank and bond market tripled the financing of foreign corporations in their operations in this country. Why do the banks lend to the huge, foreign companies operating in Canada? Basically, they do it for two reasons; one is for the security of their loan and the second is that it provides them with great profits. Canadian banks have been operating with tremendous profits in the last two years. Profits have approximately doubled those in the non-financial sector of the business world. From 1967 to 1971, for example, the banks' profits increased by 102 per cent. The five major banks hold some 70 corporate directorships. Of those 70 corporate directorships, about half are with foreign-owned corporations.
You can see, again, that there is a tendency throughout the whole banking and financial system for the banks to lend a great deal of money, perhaps as much as half of their funds, to foreign corporations operating either in Canada or outside the boundaries of our country. The banks also encourage the spending of Canadian money in other parts of the world. I have here, for example, a couple of advertisements from the New York Times and the Washington Post by the Toronto-Dominion Bank. The ad says, in a big headline, "We are happy to be accused of unCanadian activities". I have here another advertisement by the Royal Bank of Canada, saying in a great big headline, "We deliver Canada. Contact the healthy bank for a copy of businessmen's Canada". Again, that comes from a foreign newspaper.
What I am saying is that the banks in this country are largely responsible for the sell-out of funds, for the financing of foreign corporations in this country and for the draining of funds that are now leaving this country for other countries around the world. Our banks have 300 offices operating in 40 different countries that serve basically multinational corporations in the foreign countries. About 26 per cent of the assets of the Canadian banks are now held outside of Canada. I think that gives you an idea of the way banks are operating and how they are part of the drainage of funds and capital out of Canada.
Of the mutual funds in this country, some 38 per cent is now being invested in the United States alone. I suggest that the mutual fund market is another source of capital that could be used for the development of Canada for Canadians. So you can see that through the banks, through the bond market, through the financial institutions, through mutual funds and insurance companies we are financing our own sell-out. We are financing the purchase of Canada by foreign companies, by foreign multinational corporations mostly based in the United States.
It is not only the banks and the financial institutions that are aiding and assisting foreign corporations operating in Canada. The government, through DREE and many other programs in the Department of Industry, Trade and
Foreign Investment Review Act Commerce, gives grants to foreign-owned corporations. For example, Imperial Oil a few years ago was given a grant of $10 million to build a fertilizer plant near the city of Edmonton, Alberta. We give many tax incentives-some members of the Conservative Party have been outlining them-to foreign corporations to expand their business in Canada, be it in mining, in energy or in manufacturing fields.
I think this deals with the first fallacy, that Canada does not have enough capital. We do; we are a net exporter of capital. Even the Toronto stock exchange officials, when they appeared before the committee, said that Canada has enough funds to develop its own economy. There is no reason why we should have to rely on foreign equity capital to develop the country in which we live. I think that all we need now are some government policies, some industrial development policies to repatriate our economy.
The second myth that I think prevails in the minds of many people is that if foreign investment or ownership is to be hindered in some way, we will lose jobs. I suggest that is a lot of nonsense. I speak as a person who comes from the Prairies, where many people do not live as they do in southern Ontario and where I have seen some of the direct results of the foreign control of our economy. In my riding, in the town of Esterhazy, there is the world's largest potash mine owned by International Minerals Corporation of New Mexico. A few years ago when there was an oversupply of potash in the world and the potash company had to cut back on production. Naturally, the company made the decision that the cutback in the American plant would be less than in the Canadian plant, so they cut back to 90 per cent production in New Mexico and to 40 per cent production in Saskatchewan. It was the people in my riding who were laid off and lost their jobs.
I suggest that if this were a Canadian-owned company, perhaps the cutback would have been less severe, but because it was a branch plant and the headquarters were situated in another country, quite naturally the management protected its own people first rather than people living in another country. You find the same situation in many places around the world. For example, let us consider the International Nickel Company. In 1971 they closed down two mines in Canada, despite the fact that they were making tremendous profits. Their profit in 1970 was $102 million. The reason for the cut-down of production and closure of two mines was that there was a reduced demand for nickel in the world.
But what did they do after they closed down the two mines in Canada? They opened up new plants in Caledonia, Indonesia and Guatemala. They used some of the funds to develop the new mines in Guatemala and Indonesia from the profits they made here in Canada because it is cheaper to lay off Canadian workers and to hire labour in what are called underdeveloped countries. The multinational corporations can do this. If this were a Canadian-owned corporation, and particularly if it were publicly-owned, you would not have seen this cutback in production but, rather, a continuation and expansion of those mines because there is a demand for nickel in the world.

November 20, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
Due to the fact that we are foreign-controlled and dominated there is a lack of jobs in the area of research and development. Just today, for example, I heard of a young physicist, or chemist who is 27 to 30 years old who has reached the top of his field in Canada. If he wants to advance in his career, he will have to go to the head offices of the plant in either Pittsburgh or New York. That is another real consequence of foreign ownership in our country where many of the people who are involved in research or development jobs have to go to the parent company because most of the research and development is done in the United States, in Japan or wherever it may be.
Another area in which we lose jobs in Canada because of foreign ownership is in the export of raw materials. We export them in the most crude form, have them processed and finished elsewhere and then import the manufactured goods. We import more manufactured goods into this country than any other industrialized country. We all know that it is in manufacturing, processing and developing that most jobs are to be found. These are labour-intensive industries, not capital-intensive industries. If we can control our own economy, we can do a lot more processing of foodstuffs and of natural resources in our own country rather than exporting them in a raw state to other countries.
Take the example of Sudbury, where nickel is mined and exported in its crude state to Pittsburgh, to be refined there and provide jobs for Americans. This is another consequence of foreign ownership where we lose jobs rather than gain them simply because there is so much foreign equity in the ownership of our economy. Another consequence of this which results in our losing jobs is that when the parent country is in trouble, it will introduce a program like the U.S. DISC program. The hon. member for Crowfoot is very well aware of it. Or a bill will be introduced like the Burke-Hartke bill in an attempt to reduce foreign expansion and investment. In that case we find Canadians losing jobs because branch plants here are not expanded and preference is given to the parent companies in the United States. We have had many examples of this over the past few years.
I contend that we have enough money in this country to develop it ourselves and to provide more jobs for our people. There is one other point I wish to mention about capital. It was raised again today by one of the members of the Progressive Conservative Party who accused one of our premiers of going to New York or Washington to borrow money on the financial markets there. I am not saying that all foreign debt capital should be excluded from this country. There is a difference between equity and debt. Many states have gone to other countries to borrow money to build up their industry and after a period of time have paid off the debt and owned their industry outright. But that is not what is happening with respect to our capital requirements today. Instead of issuing mortgages, we provide equity in ownership, so that the dividends flow back to the investors in various countries.
As I said before, Mr. Speaker, there are a number of other areas in which we should be moving, beyond what is proposed in this bill. I wish to touch briefly on five or six of them before I conclude. First of all, we should have

some legislation to deal with existing corporations as they expand. Since this bill deals with only 10 per cent to 20 per cent of foreign investment activity, obviously we are missing the boat. Obviously, we are not touching any existing corporations such as Imperial Oil, General Motors and IT&T, and we will have to find ways of getting at existing corporations.
Secondly, like the hon. member for Fort William (Mr. McRae), I think we should be expanding the sector-by-sector approach to repatriating our economy. We have controls against foreign ownership in broadcasting and banking. I believe we should extend that control to the energy field because it is vital to all industry. At present, our gas and oil industry is 90 per cent owned by foreigners. All future development should not only be Canadian owned, but I would argue for its public ownership. Gas and oil are public utilities. They must be used for the benefit of the public. The industry should be operated as a public utility and run for the benefit of the people of the country. We can do that, Mr. Speaker.
The province of Alberta this year will be exporting about $1 billion in profits which will go to foreign oil companies mainly based in the United States. From my own province of Saskatchewan, which does not produce that much gas and oil, there will be an outflow of about $120 million to parent companies in the United States. What I am saying is that if we have control of the oil and gas industry, under public ownership, these profits would accrue to the people of Canada. We do have the funds in this country to undertake that. We can raise what we need. We can tax the gas and oil companies that we already have here. We can take the proceeds from export taxes. We can float bonds in this country. By using all these devices we will have enough funds to have the oil and gas industry in Canada taken into public ownership and made to serve the people of the country. All this we can do. We have the technology, we have vast reserves of gas and oil, and we have a need for them here in Canada.
The third thing we should be doing is reform the taxation system so that we do not continue to give huge tax incentives to foreign investors, particularly in the energy and mining areas. As has already been pointed out in this debate, foreign investors do have a tax advantage that Canadians do not enjoy. Fourthly, under the government's industrial policies we should enact legislation requiring resource industries in Canada, in mining and so on, to develop and process more of the raw materials in this country. This has already been done by various governments. It was done by the provincial government of Ontario in the area of pulp and paper mills. Now, timber cut in the province must be processed in the province, thus providing jobs for the people of the province. This could be done in many other industries and would provide more jobs for Canadians.
We must insist on having more research and development undertaken in Canada. Without research and development we will never make great progress in industry. At present there is not much specialization of industry in Canada. What do we produce as specialists in Canada? We produce very little because we have a branch plant economy which depends too much on the decisions made by parent corporations.
November 20, 1973

We must end a lot of the government's giveaway programs under which money goes to foreign corporations. Under the Department of Regional Economic Expansion I find that a lot of capital grants go to foreign-owned corporations. Under the IRDIA program, 39 per cent of the grants go to foreign corporations. Under the PAIT program, 45 per cent of the grants go to foreign-owned corporations. We must start to phase this out, and instead provide government assistance to Canadian corporations and citizens. A seventh suggestion I would like to make is that we use some of our foreign exchange reserves to buy back parts of the economy. Why do we not use $3 billion or $4 billion, using all these sources, to develop an allCanadian gas and oil industry, rather than having that industry developed by foreign-based, multinational corporations?
As my eighth suggestion, I say we must have more public ownership in this country and much more development undertaken through Crown corporations. This is the only way in many areas. Really, what has private enterprise done in the Maritimes? What has it done in eastern Quebec? It will not go into those parts of the country because it cannot make a buck. It will only go there if you provide it with huge incentives-and once the incentives die, the companies that are established want to bail out. A good example is Devco, in the province of Nova Scotia.
My ninth suggestion is that we must have some investment controls making it mandatory that the banks and financial institutions in Canada lend more of their funds to Canadians. My understanding is that roughly half of the loans made by Canadian banks and financial institutions go to foreigners either operating inside or outside Canada. I suggest that the government over a period of years could make it mandatory for this figure to be increased, say to 60 per cent of their funds going to Canadians in the first year, 70 per cent in the next year, 80 per cent in the next, and so on. There is no reason why we should be financing foreign corporations that take over our own companies. Another way we might do this is by establishing a Crown bank in this country to provide more competition for the other banks and operating in terms of direct investment, in terms of direct funding of Canadian enterprises. These are some of the things that could and must be done if we are to develop a country that is truly Canadian and is owned and controlled by the people.
There is another thing we could do, and it has already been done by such radical countries as Switzerland. That is, to use foreign exchange controls to keep out some foreign funds. In Switzerland there is an 8 per cent negative charge on any money that comes into the country. We could use foreign exchange controls like that in order to guide and plan the fiscal and monetary development of our country.
There are just a few things that the minister could pursue in order to repatriate the economy. The bill before us goes only part way; it only screens the acquisition of Canadian companies by foreigners and new areas of expansion. That is a very small part of the problem, Mr. Speaker. It we are to take control of our own country and grapple with the question of foreign ownership, we need policies that go much further. We have the funds and we
Foreign Investment Review Act have the technology; all we need is the planning and policies. One way of achieving that is for those of us who feel strongly about it to squeeze as much as we can out of the orange before it dries up.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Is it the view of the hon. member and his party that they would be in favour of significant tax cuts to Canadians to encourage Canadian investors, including a lower income tax level to Canadian investors, corporate tax incentives and that type of program?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think there are some inequities in the tax system vis-a-vis foreign investors in this country, but I do not think the way to solve that is by giving Canadians a much lower tax bracket or greater tax incentives. The Conservative Party has argued for years that the way to develop this country is through incentives-but that is not going to work. It is one of the reasons why development in Canada has been concentrated in southern Ontario-Montreal and Toronto. If you operate on that type of system, you will find the capital going where the market is, where transportation costs are lower, and so on. I do not think you can develop this country by providing greater handouts to businessmen, because there is not that much difference between the Canadian entrepreneur and the foreign entrepreneur.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: That is what we wanted you to say.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: I see no reason why the foreign oil man should have a greater tax advantage than his Canadian counterpart. If you want to develop this country, you can do it by cutting the tax of the low income person or average income person. He will then spend more, he will need more consumer items and the economy will grow. This is one way to stimulate the economy. If a person can afford to buy another car, I am sure General Motors will not complain.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I was interested in the reply given by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) to the question put by the hon. member for Peel South (Mr. Blenkarn) with regard to incentives. If I heard him correctly, he said that incentive goes where the trade is; that money will search out the best place. He felt it would probably go to southwestern Ontario, or somewhere in Ontario, where the money already is. He would know what the situation is if he lived in the province of Alberta. In fact, he does not have to live there; he just has to use the telephone, which the government provides for him, to phone a real estate agent in Alberta. Nine out of ten of them are getting requests for

November 20, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act opportunities to invest money from British Columbia, so there is some kind of drift of money out of B.C. to Alberta.
Any real estate agent in Alberta will tell you that in the last ten days he has had requests for opportunities to invest money in Alberta. There seems to be greater incentive there, or there seems disincentive in the province of British Columbia. The hon. member's party should try to find out why the flood of money is coming from British Columbia to Alberta. It certainly would be an awakening truth for his party to analyse that problem.
I ask him to just get on the phone tomorrow to any real estate agent in the telephone book in Alberta and ask if he has had any requests to invest money from British Columbia in the province. The answer will be, "lots of it". We are having a hard time placing it, Mr. Speaker, but we want it and we will do our best to sell them something. The hon. member spoke about the outflow of capital. There is nothing in this bill to prevent capital going out of Canada. But he said it four or five times. I generally repeat myself three times, but he beat me. All the mutual funds in Canada are finding some other source to develop their money, according to him.
The oddity of this piece of legislation is that it will encourage further outflow of capital. This afternoon the minister said there is one view, that government should not interfere in business, and there is another view that government should. He said he was one of those who thought that government should interfere. Is this going to encourage Canadian money to stay at home? I do not think so. Certainly money will seek the highest return. In the past, government intervention with major investors in Canada has caused concern to some individuals. Their hands have been burned because of government intervention; and if they have money to invest when this agency is set up, they are going to seek another country.
While the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville may have been making a point which school children could have understood, we in this House surely understand what it is going to do. We understand that it will encourage a greater outflow of capital. He talked about how we should develop processing in Canada. Of course we should, but we must have the capital to invest in the country. Then, when we have developed the processing, we have to find the markets. Saskatchewan has been traditional in the export of its raw material. What is its biggest raw material, exported for huge amounts of money? Wheat-and they get it out of there as quickly as they can. Feed barley goes out as well. They do not even want to feed it to their own cattle and have given no encouragement to invest in a feed plant in the province.
The hon. member said that the potash industry was in a terrible situation; that at one time there was a surplus of potash and foreign companies curtailed the production in Saskatchewan, and that if potash had been owned by a public company there would have been no curtailment. What nonsense, Mr. Speaker. He said there was a world surplus of potash. Naturally, the potash that is the most costly to produce is the first to gc out of production. Naturally, if there is a surplus of potash and the price is low, it will not be produced no matter whether a Canadian or an international company is involved in its production.

A company will only produce something when the price is right. If there is a surplus of any commodity and the price goes down, it will not be produced. The Alberta Wheat Pool and the Calgary Wheat Pool were producing fertilizer in Calgary. When the LIFT program was introduced and the use of fertilizer in Canada was cut back, you should have seen what happened. The hon. member for Yorkton-Melville should have visited the plant. He would have seen the surpluses piled up. He knows what the Alberta and Saskatchewan wheat pools did. They had surpluses, which they stockpiled in my constituency- good old Crowfoot. We encouraged them to stay in business. If those people had listened to people like the hon. member for Saskatoon-Biggar (Mr. Gleave), that co-operative fertilizer plant in Calgary would have been in severe difficulties.
Members of the NDP have implied that encouraging foreign investment in Canada is a sin and that only the Conservative Party wants to encourage it. What was the Saskatchewan government doing when it asked the Roumanians to build a tractor plant in Moose Jaw or Saskatoon? The people representing Moose Jaw and Saskatoon were going to Russia and to Roumania trying to get that plant established in this country. The Saskatchewan government was to give them everything under the sun in order to encourage them to invest in the province.
Odd as it may appear, Roumania said, "No, we do not want to invest in your country because you want to sell our tractors to the United States, and we do not want our tractors to go to the United States." The Saskatchewan government said that such manufacturing plant cannot be viable unless it is prepared to market its product in the United States. Isn't that odd? Because the Saskatchewan government said, "You must sell in the United States," that Roumanian plant was not established in this country. What does this mean? In this House we are speaking about the outflow of Canadian capital. The NDP members of the House want to build a fence around us; they want Canada to become an isolationist state. At the same time, the NDP government of Saskatchewan says we must sell in the United States. There is a mix-up in the thinking of the NDP. They should reconsider their position.
Canada is a trading nation. Nearly 80 per cent of Canadians, directly or indirectly, work in industries that are export-oriented. What about the automotive industry? It is 99 per cent owned by foreigners, yet the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) treads lightly there. The equity control, even of the automotive parts industry, lies not in Canada but in the United States. The NDP skirts around that question.
In our complex world we need multinational companies to market commodities. If you want to break into the Japanese meat market, the little butcher on Wellington Street will not do it. Only somebody with the finances and time can break into that market. That means a multinational company. Even the lovable farm boy, who may or may not know anything about the exporting of meat-I am inclined to think he knows very little-could break into that market. Whether we like it or not, it takes a multinational corporation to do that kind of thing. Many of those companies serve a useful purpose-

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Some are Canadian.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
-and many multinational corporations are Canadian multinational corporations. Surely we should not say, "you have grown too big; you have cut mama's apron strings and we are not going to look after you and claim to be your parents any longer." This is what this bill could do to many Canadian multinational corporations. We should have enough confidence in ourselves as Canadians to claim the parentage of the multinational corporations which have sprung from Canadian soil. We should be proud of their endeavours and use them to assist in the marketing of our goods.
The leader of the NDP suggested that Canadians have no confidence in themselves and that is why they need foreign money coming to do all these things for them. I consider that the reverse is true. Canadians have confidence in themselves and are prepared to use foreign capital to develop this country. They are not afraid. They do not need to shelter themselves. What person doing anything in Canada today is not doing it on borrowed money? There are very few. It is far easier to use money today than to use brawn. That is one thing my father taught me-although he taught me how to use brawn, too-and that is that you must have confidence in yourself to use someone else's capital, to use the banks and, if necessary, to use foreign capital.
I was very annoyed when the leader of the NDP talked about our energy industry. He said this bill will affect only a small portion of foreign investment in Canada, that it is just a short step, and that ultimately it may affect between 10 and 20 per cent-I think that is the figure he mentioned-of corporations. When he says that this bill is just a short step, he frightens Canadian investors and foreign investors in Canada. When he makes such utterances, we see a government wagged by the tail of the dog; we see a government kowtowing to the little group on my left which says that this is just a short step, that it will only affect up to 20 per cent of corporations and that it wants stricter laws.
Such utterances will make it mighty difficult to keep Canadian capital at home. They have not kept it in Saskatchewan, and are not keeping it in British Columbia. The Premier of Manitoba is doing a much better job in encouraging investment in Manitoba. He invited the Japanese over. He wants Japanese investment in Manitoba. He is not as narrow-minded and shortsighted as are certain people in this House, especially in the NDP.
The hon. member for York South suggested that oil and gas are in short supply in the Maritimes because in 1961 the Conservative government drew the Ottawa Valley line and said that western oil could be marketed as far west as the Ottawa Valley line but no farther east. He said that action has created the present high gas and oil prices in the maritimes. Well, every intelligent person in this House knows that the opposite is true. The hon. member knew it when he said it: he knows that exactly the opposite is true. It is terrible the way some people will play political games in an effort to scoop more votes. They do not consider what is good for Canada: Canada comes second to votes. I say that in view of the hypocritical statements which were made this afternoon by members such as the hon. member for York South.
Foreign Investment Review Act
The fact is that the creation of the Ottawa Valley line in 1961 enabled oil companies in Alberta which had been producing at less than 50 per cent of capacity to produce at least at 50 per cent of capacity. We wanted to build a pipeline to Montreal but were not able to do so. We said, "All right; give us a certain part of the market." Certain Canadian-owned companies were going broke, not having the resources to keep active in the Alberta oil business. Throughout the sixties these conditions brought about a reduction in the number of Canadian companies operating in the Alberta oil business. They were not able to sell enough oil and could not produce at even 50 per cent of capacity. Then along came the Ottawa Valley line. As a result, certain of the bigger companies developed the oil industry, exploration went on and to a certain extent at least that is responsible for our present increased reserves. We could assist eastern Canada with its needs if only we had the mechanical means of getting the oil there.
The leader of the New Democratic Party went on to say how terrible it is that Alberta is selling out the tar sands to foreign-owned interests. What sort of rubbish is that? Who can he convince that that is anywhere near the truth?
I surely hope it is no one in this House. The Alberta tar sands consist of 15,000 squares miles. I ask my friends to the left to envisage that. The Syncrude project, which we in Alberta all hope will go ahead, is for the right to mine eight square miles over the next 25 years. They readily admit it will require a $1 billion expenditure to put them in the position of mining those eight square miles over the next 25 years. They hope their production will be 125,000 barrels of oil a day.
When the NDP say that because of Syncrude we are selling out our natural resources to foreign investors, that is puppycock. I say puppycock because they are puppies in the investment world. Not one in their group has invested a five-cent piece in Canada. The leader of that group said they represent the average Canadian. They do not represent the average Canadian because the average Canadian has invested in Canada.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: After the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville was elected, he attended university for the first two years he was here. He has never held a job. He has not done a thing. As far as I know, he has not put a nickel into Canada. By the way he talks, I doubt if he will ever save a nickel to put into Canada.

speechtext: He is saving to go to Chile.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
The Alberta and Quebec ministers recently discussed the energy problem. There is no doubt the Alberta government will encourage Quebec to invest in another eight square miles of the tar sands. If it wants, the Ontario government can invest in another eight square miles. We will require a major capital investment in those 15,000 square miles of oil sands if all of Canada, including Quebec and the Maritimes, is to become self-sufficient. We must become self-sufficient because we can no longer trust our sources in the Middle East. We hear the hue and cry about the terrible multinational, foreign-

November 20, 1973
Foreign Investment Review Act
owned oil companies. Well, I would rather trust them today than the Arabs.
If the Canadian government wants to form an oil company to mine specifically in the Athabasca tar sands, that is a decision they will have to make. However, I would not want to see them trotting around speculating as to where the best political hay might be made. Because they want to get votes in Newfoundland, they should not drill a well off the Grand Banks. Maybe they are drilling for votes rather than oil.
The tar sands is a different situation. It is a known product that is there. If the government wants to mine there, let them put up $1 billion and get into the business. There is all kinds of oil there. One cubic yard will yield a barrel of oil. This is refined down to three-quarters of a barrel of light density crude. Squeeze out these cubic yards and you will have oil for a month or two. Everyone can go there. There is no problem; the oil is there. Let us not hear any more about Alberta selling out to foreign interests. We are still in the experimental stage of squeezing that oil out of the tar sands. We have not proven to the world that we can get that oil out of the tar sands. For the past five years, Great Canadian Oil has been involved in this and has lost money every year. To date, they have lost a total of $90 million, not counting the capitalization to get them started.

speakerposition: Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: What was the average price of crude?

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
It has not been very high for the past five years. We hope this government will allow it to be high enough in the next one, two or three years so that the oil sands can be developed and we can become self-sufficient. If we do not become self-sufficient we will be at the mercy of the Arabs until hell freezes over. If we are to become self-sufficient, the government must encourage investment in these tar sands. Don't buy this puppycock from people who are reluctant even to invest in their own province.
We hear a great deal of talk about money flowing out of the country. Certainly, money will flow out of the country. Four wells in the North Sea have more reserves than has been developed conventionally in Canada to date. In Alberta we have been drilling quite succesfully for the past 25 years.

speakerposition: Deputy Whip of the Progressive Conservative Party
subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Forty years.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext:
I know it has been longer than 25. In the past 25 years we have developed a certain amount of reserves. However, as I said, four wells in the North Sea have as much reserves as all the wells that have been drilled conventionally in Alberta. That gives some idea where the money will go if we curtail it. It will not go to develop our oil fields.
There has not been a major find of oil in Canada for nearly six years. You cannot acknowledge that fact and then continue to discourage foreign investment in oil. They are discouraged enough. Outside of the tar sands there has not been a major find for six years. In spite of this we still hear all this garbage and see government intervention in the industry. Are we to sit idly by hoping

that some day we, even with that kind of discouragement, will become self-sufficient in oil? I doubt it.
We must also consider the cost. It is obvious, and I know Your Honour will agree with me, that the first oil find is the easiest. The next find is the next easiest. For the past 25 years oil has been quite successfully found in Alberta. However, as the years go by the finds will be more difficult and more costly. That is pointed out in a brief that was sent to all parties by the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada. On page 53 it states:
In 1968, production cost per barrel was 43 cents, development cost 28 cents, and finding cost $2.63 for a total of $3.34 to replace a barrel of oil in a developed field.
That was only five years ago. What has happened since then? This year there was a 10 per cent increase in inflation. Last year there was a 10 per cent increase in inflation. All this was due to bad financial handling by the whole Department of Finance.

subsubtopic: PROVISIONS RESPECTING ACQUISITIONS OF CONTROL OF CANADIAN BUSINESS ENTERPRISES AND ESTABLISHMENT OF NEW BUSINESSES
speechtext: Hear, hear!
