speechtext:
That, coupled with six years of no major find in Alberta and greater and greater finding costs, means the following were the costs in 1972: the development costs were $2.70; finding costs were $10.98, with production costs still at a relatively stable 50 cents per barrel; replacement cost last year was $14.18 per barrel, or almost double the new posted price for Venezuelan oil. I can say it is an exaggeration. I can say I do not believe it. But if I seriously want to help Canada become self-sufficient in oil, I must put some faith in these figures. They are the best I can get.
I do not know what it costs to produce a barrel of oil, but this is what they tell me. I have to pay some attention because I know oil companies are pulling out of the east coast. I know they made five major finds of oil off Sable Island. Since they are offshore, they would not be economic to produce. In any case, no settlement has been reached as to which government the companies would be dealing with. They do not know. We proudly say we want to become self-sufficient in oil. But we are still sadly lacking in an energy policy which would go any way toward enabling us to become self-sufficient in oil in the near future.
In 1969 the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada came to Ottawa and said it wanted to build a pipeline to Montreal. The answer was no. It was told Montreal wanted to stay with Middle East and Venezuelan oil. In effect, the association was told, "Go peddle your oil elsewhere". Can you blame them for searching out the market? The industry needs a cash flow in order to offset the expense of exploring and drilling for new supplies.
The spokesman for the small NDP group to my left tries to suggest he knows nothing about energy. He knows a lot more than he admitted. He knows enough to distort the facts. He knows enough to destroy the truth in the hope that doing so may gather him a few votes. In fact, he is copying another person who was elected to power by hook or by crook in a far away land, Germany. That person was elected to power and he used the technique of the big lie. I suggest that this little group to my left is very interested
November 20, 1973

in that technique and may well attempt to copy it in the future.
The minister told us this bill was a good one and that there are five or six results the government thinks it will achieve. He said it would provide more employment. I do not see how it will. When I was old enough to work, as a boy of ten, my dad gave me a shovel and a pitchfork-and they did not cost more than $1.50. But I have three sons and I need to buy them some pretty expensive equipment before they can go to work. What I am saying is that not much capital was needed 30 or 40 years ago to get a job, but today it takes $60,000 to create one job in Canada with any degree of permanency.
This bill does not stop the outflow of capital; it encourages the outflow of capital. I do not want governments, whether provincial or federal, to get into business, but this may be the only source of capital available if we carry on as we are doing. I do not believe governments can do things better than private corporations. The governments I have seen around here in the past 15 years have not demonstrated any great degree of efficiency in terms of goods produced per man-hour. Sometimes they have laboured long and produced very little. Sometimes they have laboured very long and tried to produce a whole lot, which has only created more problems.
There is no one more anxious than myself to see more processing of raw materials done in this country, but I do not see how the bill before us will encourage such a thing. Nor do I see how it will upgrade our natural resource industry, as the minister suggested. He said there would be greater domestic content. Very often, people have said it is all right for a provincial government to go to New York to borrow money, that it was all right for Premier Bourassa to go to New York for funds to develop James Bay because that was not equity money; it would give them no control. Let me say once again in this House that the oil industry does not exercise equity control over the oil in Alberta. If the Alberta government so decides, the oil or the gas, as the case may be, stays in the ground. The company, whether American, or British, or French-it does not matter-may have drilled a well; but if Alberta doesn't like the price it is getting out of it, the price it receives, the oil stays in the ground. And no matter what the price may be, if the conservation authority in Alberta wishes to restrict the amount of oil coming out of that well, it stays in the ground.
It is often said that 80 per cent of our oil industry is controlled in the United States. That is not right. The oil industry, that portion of it which lies in Alberta, is controlled by the Alberta energy board. The portion which lies within Saskatchewan may well be controlled by a similar board, but most of the oil in that province has not been found because investment there has been discouraged.
Whether greater domestic ownership will be brought about remains to be seen. My fear is that the bill will lead to fewer Canadian companies. The minister went on to suggest that regional development, or regional input would be increased. Well, DREE was supposed to do that. It is operated by the Department of Regional Economic Expansion. It should have solved all those problems. The former minister, the present Minister of Transport (Mr. Foreign Investment Review Act Marchand) admitted in this House that he was slightly disappointed that after a year's operation DREE had created no more than 16,000 jobs having spent "X" million dollars.
The minister who is piloting this bill through the House is too stubborn or too much of a greenhorn in his department, or too frightened by cabinet domination, to accept a sensible amendment as moved by the hon. member for Central Nova (Mr. MacKay). The amendment proposed that a copy of the notice should be sent by the agency forthwith, by registered mail, to a province or provinces likely to be significantly affected by the proposal or investment to which the notice refers. Mr. Speaker, that does not turn the legislation inside out. That does not call for any major decision. It just says that a region shall be notified.

Then the minister said that the bill would improve the quality of life in Canada. I thought he was really stretching for straws when he

November 20, 1973

dragged that one in. We in Alberta tend to think that we have a pretty high quality of life. The air is quite pure; most people are working. Our biggest trouble is to keep a lot of these people we are talking about, and their money, out. We let it come in freely, but we do sometimes worry about it. There is no danger in Alberta. But I thought the minister was really reaching when he mentioned the higher quality of life.
Some mention was also made of the DISC program. The hon. member for York South is fond of holding up the oil industry as the culprit, but what about the automotive industry? Has he talked about that? Some time ago he said the government should go down to Washington and say we will cut off our energy supply unless the United States leaves the automotive pact alone. However, the next crisis in Canada will be the automotive pact since 99 per cent of the industry is United States-owned. The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Cafik) tells me he is now driving a General Motors' car. I was pleased to hear that, though I know he was driving one of the smaller makes at one time.
There is no question that if we continue to discourage foreign investment, we are exemplifying a lack of confidence in our ability to manage foreign investment. subtopic: IMMIGRATION-POSSIBLE EXEMPTION OF IROQUOIS INDIANS WISHING TO MOVE TO CANADA FROM HAVING TO APPLY FOR LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS
IMMIGRATION-POSSIBLE EXEMPTION OF IROQUOIS INDIANS WISHING TO MOVE TO CANADA FROM HAVING TO APPLY FOR LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 29, I asked the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Andras) a question with respect to the fact that no longer will Iroquois Indians born in the United States be able to cross into Canada to settle without first applying

in the United States for landed immigrant status in Canada. I stated in my question that the directive of November 30, 1972, went contrary to the historic rights and privileges granted the Iroquois as a result of their loyalty to the Crown during the American war of independence, and that special status should be granted them with respect to crossing the border and resettling in Canada. The minister replied that it was not the policy of the immigration department to grant special status to the Iroquois, and that therefore any Iroquois born in the United States would have to apply in that country for landed immigrant status if he or she desired to settle in Canada.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, many Iroquois have over the years, indeed for nearly 200 years, moved from time to time to the United States in search of employment and have remained there for considerable periods of time. They married, had children, remained there; and these are the people I am most concerned about in this short address this evening.
In the federal constituency of Brant, which I have the honour to represent in this House, lies the Six Nations Reserve with a band list of over 10,000 persons, a great many of whom live in the United States. As a result of the November 30 directive, these people have become very upset and consider this directive just another erosion of their native rights. As you know, native North Americans guard with great pride and determination rights and privileges granted them by the Crown.
The minister in his reply also stated that Indians would be treated the same as any other group and cases would be judged on an individual basis. That is a very nice, free-flowing expression. I could certainly agree with the minister with respect to Italians, Germans or Englishmen or any other ethnic group as far as the November 30 directive is concerned. But when it comes to the Iroquois and other Indian bands, I must emphasize that I cannot agree. These people were here long before all other national groups, and in my opinion an Indian born in the United States who is also a member of a Canadian band of Indians should not have to go through the procedure of applying for landed status in the country of his forefathers.
In a letter from the minister dated October 30, 1973, the fourth paragraph reads as follows:
Canadian Indians consider that there is no need for them to follow these procedures-
That is to say, immigration laws and the November 30 directive.
-since they hold that the Jay Treaty provides them with free and unrestricted movement across the Canadian-United States border. The Jay Treaty has of course no application in so far as Canadian law is concerned. In fact the Supreme Court of Canada, in a case brought before it in 1956, found that the articles of the Jay Treaty and the Treaty of Ghent which were pertinent to the question did not apply in Canada since they had not been implemented or sanctioned by legislation.
In the same letter the minister did indicate that-
-in the current review of immigration legislation we will be considering the possibility of recommending changes to the Immigration Act which would admit children of Canadian Indians who were born outside Canada provided they are registered with a Canadian Indian band under the terms of the Indian Act.
November 20, 1973

I wonder how long it will take to bring about these suggested changes, in view of the fact that many sections of the Indian Act are in such disarray? Moreover, with respect to the Six Nations Reserve, the recent Ostler decision in the Supreme Court of Ontario implies, or indeed states that this reserve is not in fact a reserve and therefore does not come under the Indian Act because the Six Nations Reserve was granted in fee simple by the Crown and is not held in trust for the Indians on that reserve by the Canadian government. I suggest that the immigration and Indian affairs departments get together on this matter and clear the air as soon as possible.
In conclusion, while the Immigration Department might be finding a way out for the Iroquois and other Indian bands, one of their fundamental and historical rights has been taken away from them in principle. Those Indians on the Six Nations Reserve to whom I have spoken, including their chief elected councillor, Richard Isaac, are not at all pleased with the way the Immigration Department is treating them. This is causing concern among many of the residents of the Six Nations Reserve, or the Tuscarora township if you wish to call it that, at this time. Many of the people who live on that reserve have moved to the United States or were born in the United States and came to Canada and are now to be subjected to what I must call an indecency in terms of their having to go through the immigration provisions in order to become Canadian citizens, when in fact they were the first Canadian citizens.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: IMMIGRATION-POSSIBLE EXEMPTION OF IROQUOIS INDIANS WISHING TO MOVE TO CANADA FROM HAVING TO APPLY FOR LANDED IMMIGRANT STATUS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there has always been a certain amount of friction between North American Indians and the immigration service because of differing concepts of the Indians' position in modern North American society. These are epitomized in disputes over the effect of the Jay Treaty and the question of nationality.
In 1794, Great Britain and the United States concluded the "Treaty of Amity, Commerce and Navigation," commonly called the Jay Treaty, which says in effect that Indians living on either side of the Canada-United States border could freely cross that border into the other country. With the outbreak of the war in 1812, the United States considered the Jay Treaty abrogated, but some argue that it was restored by the Treaty of Ghent in 1815.
In 1928, the United States enacted legislation that allowed Canadian Indians to enter the United States under much the same terms as those embodied in the Jay Treaty, but Canada has not taken similar action. In fact, the Supreme Court of Canada, in a case brought before it in 1956, found that the particular articles of the Jay Treaty and the Treaty of Ghent that were pertinent to the question had no application in Canada since they had not been implemented or sanctioned by Canadian legislation, even if these treaties were valid. They were in effect treaties between Great Britain and the United States, and neither Canada nor the Indians were a party to either.
The nationality question, simply stated, is that some Indians refuse to recognize Canadian or American citizenship as applicable to them; they claim not only to be Indians first and foremost, but to be Indians only. The
Adjournment Debate
Indian Act permits an Indian to be registered as a member of a Canadian band without regard to his citizenship. The Citizenship Act accords an Indian Canadian citizenship if he is born in Canada or if he is born outside Canada to a Canadian citizen father and his birth is registered with citizenship authorities. The Immigration Act and regulations permit nearly free access to Canada by Canadian citizens, but insist on certain formalities for the entry and stay of all other categories.
The problem arises when a Canadian Indian returns to Canada, after a period in the United States, with a U.S. born spouse or children. If the Canadian Indian is a male and a member of a Canadian band, his wife and children may be registered under the Indian Act as members of the band. Under the Citizenship Act, however, the wife cannot become a Canadian citizen until a year after her admission as a landed immigrant. In the meantime, she remains an American citizen regardless of her status under the Indian Act. The children may be Canadian citizens if the fact of their birth abroad to a Canadian father is registered with the citizenship authorities but, if not, the children also remain American citizens. Under the Immigration Act, in turn, the wife and children, as American citizens coming to Canada to live, must be treated as immigrants, again regardless of their status under the Indian Act.
At a recent meeting with a group of Indian leaders, including Carl Brant, president of the Iroquois and Allied Indian Association, this whole matter was discussed and two very valuable avenues of approach were agreed upon. Firstly, Indian leaders will be urged to submit their suggestions on this subject to the task force reviewing current immigration legislation. Secondly, a meeting of the assistant deputy minister, Indian and Eskimo affairs, the assistant deputy minister of immigration and a senior representative of the Secretary of State will be held to determine if the registration of Indian children born abroad as members of an Indian band can be tied to the registration of births abroad for citizenship purposes.

subtopic: ENERGY-AUTHORITY OF GOVERNMENT TO ENFORCE PETROLEUM PRICE FREEZE AND PRICE INDEXING
ENERGY-AUTHORITY OF GOVERNMENT TO ENFORCE PETROLEUM PRICE FREEZE AND PRICE INDEXING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, tonight I draw your attention to a question I directed to the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) on November 2 in connection with the purported freeze by this government on petroleum prices and as to whether the government felt it had the authority. I also referred to the activity of the government in disciplining oil companies if they decided on their own to disobey the freeze, if indeed there was one.
The Prime Minister brushed aside my question and sort of indicated that the government had the authority to control prices, in spite of the fact that I asked the question because in answer to previous questions he indicated that there was perhaps some doubt in that prices could only be controlled by provinces under the heading of "property and civil rights". Clearly, the Government of Canada has the authority under the "peace, order and good government" provisions of our constitution to control prices in the national sense.
However, what has happened is not control of prices but total sham, because not one iota of legislation has been

November 20, 1973
Adjournment Debate
introduced to this House entitling this government to control petroleum prices. We have been told that there is a price freeze and that the price freeze will last until January 31, 1974. But in fact there is no price freeze because there has been no legislation authorizing a price freeze. It is a voluntary action, it is not law. The rules that are voluntarily asked of the industry are meaningless-zip!
When the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Mr. Macdonald) was speaking to the House on November 1, he said that Gulf Canada had not obeyed the petroleum price freeze and they were bad corporate citizens. I do not want to defend major oil companies here tonight. On many occasions I have criticized the activities of these corporations in dealing with service station operators and the like. To some extent they are monopolistic. However, they are corporate citizens of this country. Gulf Canada in particular has a fairly large refinery in my constituency.
That corporation is a good corporate citizen in Mississauga. It allows its employees time off at full pay to run scouting ventures and other community activities. It contributes to the tax base of Mississauga. It tries to keep a clean ship and it is a good corporate citizen. But what does this minister say about the company? He says it is an American company run by an American president, and that it would not obey the "non-law". When, in the history of this country, has disobeying the edict of a government that has no authority and has not requested the authority from this House been to act as a bad corporate citizen?
Here we have a purported price freeze when in fact there is no price freeze. Here we have a company told that they are bad boys because they did not obey a law that does not exist. What kind of newspeak have we arrived at here? Here we have a government that says, "You have done wrong because we say you did wrong. Not because parliament said you did wrong, not because there is a law that says you disobeyed it, but because we in our wisdom say you have done wrong." According to press reports, the NDP has suggested that if the price freeze does not extend beyond March 31 it will vote against the government. Through you, Sir, I would like to tell the members of the NDP tonight that there is no price freeze anyway, and they can vote against the government right now and not be out of court on that score.
The government has used blackmail pressure against a corporation that is paying taxes in this country, that has obeyed every other law of this country, and has slandered that company and its president in this House where it is not subject to any of the laws of slander. The government has tried to enforce rules that do not exist and has indicated to the country that there is a freeze on petroleum prices when there is no freeze. It has not brought forth legislation. It has acted in a most irresponsible way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Mark MacGuigan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Manpower and Immigration):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Manpower and Immigration
subtopic: ENERGY-AUTHORITY OF GOVERNMENT TO ENFORCE PETROLEUM PRICE FREEZE AND PRICE INDEXING
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on September 4 the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) announced in the House that the oil industry would be asked to refrain from further increases to Canadian consumers before January 30, 1974. On the basis of this voluntary program there has been a good response from industry and to date there has in fact been no need for a

legislative base for the program. The government started out with the concept of a voluntary program, which has operated well and there is no need to consider empowering legislation for the term of the program as now envisaged. As the Prime Minister said today in the House: "We had obtained agreement from the major petroleum companies to accept a voluntary freeze until that date. This is the undertaking I gave and this is the undertaking which I believe they intend respecting."
I would further draw the hon. member's attention to the comments of the Prime Minister this afternoon concerning the lifting of the freeze and government policy attendant thereto. The Prime Minister indicated that members of the House "should be in a position to know the government policy related thereto in some detail and assess for themselves, perhaps in advance of February 1, what the effect might be."
I would just add, Mr. Speaker, that the objection which I understand the minister had to the action of Gulf Canada in advancing prices at the time it did was not that it was forbidden by law to do it, but that it had agreed with the Government of Canada that it would not do so; and it was precisely the breaking of an agreement with the Government of Canada, and not the breaking of a law, which well merited the condemnation of the minister.

subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-ACCELERATED COVERAGE PLAN-DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION
CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-ACCELERATED COVERAGE PLAN-DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on October 24, 1973, I asked the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) about the five-year accelerated coverage plan the objective of which is to bring radio and television coverage to all unserved communities in Canada with populations of 500 or more, and whether this plan had been submitted to the cabinet for consideration and approval. He indicated to me that it had not been submitted to the cabinet for approval.
I should like to state that people in the north have had aspirations for television-radio coverage for many years. Politicians have been making them promises for years- politicians from both the old-line parties who happen to have been in power for years. I might also point out that on December 4, 1972, I received a letter from the CBC and I quote one paragraph from it:
A number of improvements are envisaged in our future plans for the constituency of Meadow Lake. We plan to establish television rebroadcasting transmitters at Leoville, Green Lake, Dorin-tosh, Goodsoil, Beauval, Michel and La Loche. In future development of radio service, transmitters at Beauval, Buffalo Narrows and La Loche are envisaged. As all of these projects and hundreds of others across Canada are part of a master plan yet to be submitted to the government for final approval, we cannot yet be specific about the exact time at which they will be activated.
Several months later, in March of 1973 to be exact, I brought up this matter again and the minister, in a memo to me, indicated as follows:
The corporation has just recently finalized its five-year accelerated coverage plan whose aim is to bring radio and television coverage in the required language to all unserved communities in Canada with a population of 500 or more. The plan will be reviewed by the CBC board of directors at its forthcoming meet-
November 20, 1973

ing on March 26. If approved as presented, the plan will then be submitted to the Secretary of State.
Apparently the CBC has its plan finalized and it has been submitted to the Secretary of State, but I was wondering what the delay is in submitting it to cabinet and getting final approval on this project. One of the most obvious needs of northern Saskatchewan is radio and television service. At present, the only radio transmitter in northern Saskatchewan is a 40-watt relay station at Uranium City which broadcasts programs from the CBC northern service station in Yellowknife. Low-power television transmitters are operational in La Ronge, from CBC Saskatoon via microwave, and Uranium City from CBC Vancouver via satellite. Now the station in Uranium City is experiencing a great deal of problems as well, in that originally they were getting only programs from Vancouver and now they are getting programs from Vancouver and Halifax and other places in Canada, and in some cases programs have been repeated as many as three times a day.
Except for these two limited facilities, residents have either no service at all or poor and erratic reception of stations, often from other provinces or from outside of Canada. Owing to this situation, I am concerned that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation has not sought licensing approval to extend radio and television service to other northern areas in Saskatchewan.
The CBC has presented an extended coverage plan to the federal cabinet to provide their services to unserviced communities of 500 population or more over a five-year period, and as yet the federal cabinet is holding back on its approval and I feel that the time has come to approve it immediately. Broadcasting facilities at some of the points I mentioned earlier in my speech would do much to overcome the lack of media service now available. There are other unserviced communities meeting the criteria of "500 population" that have not been included in the CBC listing.
Delays in receiving approval of the extended coverage plan have apparently not stalled service extensions in other northern regions. At least five communities in northern Manitoba are scheduled to receive television service this year. New radio and television transmitters are also operational or under way in northern Alberta, the Northwest Territories and the Yukon. I applaud these extensions but believe that immediate consideration of the needs of northern Saskatchewan must also be made by the CBC.
Population figures would suggest that some smaller centres in other northern regions have been given priority over Saskatchewan communities. There are several northern Saskatchewan communities with populations of at least 1,000 lacking reliable radio reception and no television service at all: for example, Stanley Mission, with a population of 1,000; lie a la Crosse-Beauval, with a population of 1,800; Portage La Loche, population 1,800; Buffalo Narrows, population 1,300; La Ronge, population 2,800. The extension of television service to La Ronge this summer was much appreciated, but the community's radio reception remains very poor.
In view of the fact that attempts are being made to develop northern Saskatchewan economically, I consider
Adjournment Debate
that the extension of radio and television service must proceed with urgency. I believe that in addition to providing news, entertainment and educational programming, electronic media can contribute in developing community awareness, interest and action necessary to facilitate meaningful northern progress. Ideally, it is hoped that the CBC plans for Saskatchewan might include establishment of a radio program centre in the north somewhat similar to that provided in locations such as Frobisher Bay, Inuvik or Churchill. Such a station could feed transmitters throughout northern Saskatchewan and would provide a worth-while blend of national, regional and local programming.
It should be indicated that the government of Saskatchewan is proceeding with the extension of microwave facilities in the north. Saskatchewan Telecommunications is completing service extensions to Buffalo Narrows and Wollaston Lake this year and will complete their program as far north as La Roche and Uranium City in 1974.
The distribution mechanism for radio and television signals is therefore available to service CBC transmitters, and now all the CBC has to do is co-operate with the government of Saskatchewan to use the facilities already there. I understand that the government of Saskatchewan is anxious to co-operate in any way possible to expedite CBC extension to northern Saskatchewan. I sincerely hope that the minister will expedite this program, which is an excellent one, as quickly as possible.
[ Translation]

speakeroldname: Mr. Gilles Marceau (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Secretary of State of Canada
subtopic: CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION-ACCELERATED COVERAGE PLAN-DATE OF IMPLEMENTATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, first I should like to congratulate the previous speaker for his excellent remarks and especially for the very moderate way in which he made his important representations, which I shall naturally transmit to the minister.
I should also like to thank him for allowing me to say that I share his interest in the accelerated program which I hope will soon be implemented. Unfortunately, certain strategic areas of the country still lack the French or English radio and television stations which could reflect throughout the provinces the cultures of which Canada is rightfully proud.
I believe that one of the main purposes of the CBC is to work for a greater unity of all Canadians and I am completely in favour of this rather far-reaching program.
I believe that I should explain to my hon. friend that while we may agree about the principle of the project, it is extremely important that we should determine its terms and conditions.
